relationship: parallel dating to Jehoiakim's fourth year
rationale: Both introductions date a divine word to the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah. The matching royal name, parentage and regnal year connect the settings without making the two speeches identical.
source_text: The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all Judah’s people in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah,

target_units.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the Lord’s word came to me:

relationship: repeated dating of Jeremiah's prophetic beginning
rationale: The twenty-three-year retrospective begins in Josiah's thirteenth year. The book's opening likewise dates God's word to Jeremiah to the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amos, confirming the stated starting point.
source_text: In the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amos, king of Judah, and until this day, twenty-three years, I spoke to you, rising early and saying,

target_units.text: which became God’s word to him in the days of Josiah son of Amos, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.

relationship: parallel rejection of repeatedly sent prophets
rationale: Both describe God rising early and sending prophetic messengers to His people. Jeremiah stresses failure to listen, while Chronicles specifies their mockery and rejection of the messengers and words.
source_text: and I was sending My servants the prophets to you, sending from early morning, and you did not listen or attend with your ears,

target_units.text: The Lord, the God of their fathers, sent through prophets, rising early and sending His messengers, because He spared His people and His sanctuary.
They kept sneering at His messengers, treating His words as nothing, and mocking His prophets, until the Lord’s anger rose among His people, until there was no healing.

relationship: parallel repentance linked with continued dwelling in the given land
rationale: Both call for corrected ways and practices and connect that response with dwelling in the land given to the fathers. Jeremiah 7 expands the required conduct into justice, protection of vulnerable people and rejection of foreign gods.
source_text: saying: Turn, each from his evil way and from your evil practices, and you will dwell upon the land I gave to you and your fathers from age to age.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, Israel’s God: Correct your ways and your practices, and I will settle you in this place.
Do not put your confidence in yourselves on false words, because they will not benefit you at all when they say, ‘The Lord’s temple, the Lord’s temple it is.’
For if you truly correct your ways and practices and truly execute judgment between a man and his neighbor,
and do not oppress a newcomer, orphan, or widow, and do not shed innocent blood in this place, and do not follow foreign gods to your own harm,
then I will settle you in this place, in the land I gave your fathers, from age to age.

relationship: parallel prohibition of foreign gods with a warning of divine anger
rationale: Jeremiah forbids following, serving and bowing to foreign gods, lest the people's works provoke harm. Deuteronomy likewise forbids following other gods and warns that the Lord's anger may bring destruction.
source_text: Do not follow foreign gods to serve them and bow down to them, so that you do not provoke Me by your hands’ works into harming you.

target_units.text: You shall not go after other gods, of the gods of the nations round about you,
for the Lord your God in the midst of you is a jealous God; lest the Lord your God be kindled to wrath against you, and destroy you from the face of the earth.

relationship: parallel unbelief leading to divine judgment
rationale: Jeremiah identifies refusal to believe God's words as the reason for the judgment announced in the following unit. Hebrews similarly explains the wilderness generation's exclusion from rest through unbelief, while describing a different generation and penalty.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Since you did not believe My words,

target_units.text: For who, having heard, provoked Him? Was it not all who came out of Egypt through Moses?
And with whom was He indignant for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?
And to whom did He swear that they would not enter His rest, except those who disobeyed?
And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.

relationship: parallel northern invasion as judgment
rationale: Jeremiah 25 announces a clan brought from the north against the land and surrounding nations. Jeremiah 6 likewise announces a northern people and nations arrayed for war against Zion, supplying a particular northern-invasion counterpart.
source_text: behold, I am sending and will take the clan from the north and bring them against this land, its inhabitants, and all the surrounding nations. I will lay them waste and make them a ruin, a hissing, and eternal reproach.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people comes from the north, and nations will be roused from the earth’s extremity.
They will grasp bow and spear; it is ruthless and will show no mercy. Its voice is like a surging sea; on horses and chariots it will draw up like fire for war against you, daughter of Zion.

relationship: repeated removal of gladness and wedding voices
rationale: Both judgments remove sounds of joy and the voices of bridegroom and bride from the land. Jeremiah 25 additionally names ointment's fragrance and a lamp's light; these details are not supplied by the target.
source_text: And I will remove from them the sound of joy and delight, the sound of bridegroom and bride, the fragrance of ointment and the light of a lamp.

target_units.text: And I will stop the sound of those rejoicing and the sound of those glad, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride, from Judah’s cities and Jerusalem’s thoroughfares, because the whole land will become a desolation.

relationship: explicit later consultation of Jeremiah's seventy-year period
rationale: Jeremiah announces seventy years of desolation and service among nations. Daniel explicitly considers books concerning Jeremiah and a seventy-year term for Jerusalem's reproach, connecting his calculation with Jeremiah's prophetic period.
source_text: And all the land will become a ruin, and they will serve among the nations for seventy years.

target_units.text: in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, considered in the books the number of years, when a command came to the land concerning Jeremiah the prophet, to bring Jerusalem’s reproach to its full term: seventy years.

relationship: historical account connecting deportation and seventy years with Jeremiah
rationale: Chronicles describes deported survivors serving Babylon's rulers and identifies seventy years of the land's desolation with the Lord's word through Jeremiah. It adds the land's Sabbath observance to the service and desolation announced here.
source_text: And all the land will become a ruin, and they will serve among the nations for seventy years.

target_units.text: He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,
to fulfill the Lord’s word through Jeremiah’s mouth, until the land accepted its Sabbaths, to keep Sabbath. All the days of its desolation it kept Sabbath, to complete seventy years.

relationship: complementary outcomes associated with Babylon's seventy years
rationale: Jeremiah 25 announces judgment upon the nation when seventy years are fulfilled. Jeremiah 36 promises a visit and return for the exiles when Babylon's seventy years are about to be fulfilled, describing the people's restoration alongside the judgment announcement.
source_text: And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will exact justice from that nation, says the Lord, and make them an everlasting ruin.

target_units.text: Because thus said the Lord: When seventy years are about to be fulfilled for Babylon, I will visit you and establish My words for you, to return your people to this place.

relationship: parallel recording of Jeremiah's words concerning nations
rationale: The composite unit announces execution of the words written in the book and identifies Jeremiah's prophecies against the nations. Jeremiah 43 commands a writing roll containing the delivered oracles concerning Jerusalem, Judah and all nations.
source_text: And I will bring upon that land all My words that I spoke against it, everything written in this book. What Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.

target_units.text: Take a writing roll and write on it all the words I have delivered to you as oracles concerning Jerusalem, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah king of Judah until today.

relationship: parallel breaking of a nation's bow
rationale: Elam's bow, associated with its dominion, is to be shattered. Hosea likewise announces the shattering of Israel's bow in Jezreel alongside an end to its kingdom; the nations and locations remain distinct.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Let Elam’s bow be shattered, the beginning of their dominion.

target_units.text: The Lord said to him, “Call him Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge Jezreel’s blood upon Jehu’s house and put an end to the kingdom of Israel’s house.
On that day I will shatter Israel’s bow in the Valley of Jezreel.”

relationship: parallel scattering of survivors to every wind
rationale: Jeremiah threatens Elam with four winds from heaven's ends and dispersal among them. Ezekiel likewise announces scattering Jerusalem's survivors to every wind, with sword judgment accompanying the dispersal.
source_text: I will bring upon Elam four winds from heaven’s four ends and scatter them among all these winds. There will be no nation where Elam’s outcasts do not come.

target_units.text: Therefore fathers will eat children in your midst, and children will eat fathers. I will execute judgments against you and scatter all your survivors to every wind.
Therefore, as I live, says the Lord, surely, because you defiled My holy places with all your abominations, I too will reject you. My eye will not spare, and I too will have no mercy.

A quarter of you will be consumed by death; a quarter of you will perish by famine within you; a quarter of you I will scatter to every wind; and a quarter of you will fall by the sword around you, and I will draw a sword after them.

relationship: repeated sword pursuit until consumption
rationale: After Elam's scattering, Jeremiah 25 threatens a sword sent after them until they are consumed. Jeremiah 9 uses the same combination of scattering among nations and a sword sent until consumption, there addressing the people who abandoned God's law.
source_text: I will terrify them before their enemies who seek their lives and bring calamities upon them according to the anger of My wrath. I will send My sword after them until they are consumed.

target_units.text: and I will scatter them among nations that neither they nor their fathers knew, and send the sword upon them until I consume them by it.

relationship: related divine throne and rule over nations
rationale: God promises to set His throne in Elam while removing its king and nobles. The psalm likewise joins God's rule over nations with His sitting upon a holy throne, clarifying the international sovereignty expressed by the image.
source_text: I will set My throne in Elam and send king and nobles away from there.

target_units.text: God reigned over the nations; God sits upon His holy throne.

relationship: parallel restoration of a foreign nation's captivity after judgment
rationale: Jeremiah promises to turn back Elam's captivity in the last days. Ezekiel similarly promises to gather scattered Egyptians and turn back their captivity, but gives a forty-year period and a lowly restored dominion rather than Elam's formulation.
source_text: In the last days I will turn back Elam’s captivity, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: After forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations where they were scattered,
and I will turn back the captivity of the Egyptians and settle them in the land of Pathros, in the land from which they were taken; it will be a lowly dominion
among all the dominions; it will no longer be exalted over the nations, and I will make them few, so that they are not more numerous among the nations.

relationship: related account of Babylon's seizure of Egyptian territory
rationale: Jeremiah names Babylon's defeat of Pharaoh Neco's force at Carchemish beside the Euphrates. Kings reports that Babylon took Egypt's territory up to the Euphrates, supplying a related geopolitical account without naming this battle or Neco.
source_text: For Egypt, concerning the force of Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt, who was beside the Euphrates River at Carchemish and whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck in the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah:

target_units.text: The king of Egypt did not again leave his land, because the king of Babylon had taken everything belonging to the king of Egypt from Egypt’s torrent to the River Euphrates.

relationship: parallel military preparation with weapons and shields
rationale: Jeremiah commands taking weapons and shields and advancing to war. Ezekiel describes Gog's assembled force with shields and swords and commands its preparation; the shared equipment and mobilization do not identify the two armies.
source_text: Take up weapons and shields, and advance to war!

target_units.text: and I will gather you and all your force, horses and horsemen all clothed in breastplates, a great assembly, small shields, helmets and swords,
Persians, Ethiopians and Libyans, all with helmets and small shields;
Gomer and all those around him, the house of Thergama from the farthest north and all those around him, and many nations with you.
Be made ready; prepare yourself, you and all your assembly gathered with you, and you will be a guard for Me.

relationship: parallel equipment of mounted forces
rationale: Jeremiah's preparation names horses, riders, helmets and breastplates. Ezekiel's assembled force likewise includes horses and horsemen clothed in breastplates, with helmets among its equipment.
source_text: Saddle the horses; mount, riders! Take your positions in your helmets. Hold your spears forward; put on your breastplates!

target_units.text: and I will gather you and all your force, horses and horsemen all clothed in breastplates, a great assembly, small shields, helmets and swords,

relationship: parallel fear in judgment upon Egypt
rationale: Jeremiah asks why Egypt's fighters are terrified and retreating as their strong men are cut down. Isaiah likewise portrays Egyptians trembling before the Lord's hand and fearing when the Judeans' country is named.
source_text: Why are they terrified and withdrawing backward? Because their strong men will be cut down. They fled in flight and did not turn back, surrounded on every side, says the Lord.

target_units.text: On that day the Egyptians will be like women in fear and trembling before the Lord Sabaoth’s hand, which He Himself will bring upon them.
The Judeans’ country will become a terror to the Egyptians; whenever anyone names her to them, they will fear because of the counsel the Lord has counseled against her.

relationship: parallel failure of speed and strength to secure escape
rationale: Jeremiah denies escape to the swift and strong in the defeat beside the Euphrates. Amos similarly says flight will fail the runner, strength will fail the mighty, and the swift will not be saved.
source_text: Let the swift not flee, nor the strong man escape. Northward, in the places beside the Euphrates, they grew weak and have fallen.

target_units.text: and flight will perish from the runner, the mighty one will certainly not maintain his strength, and the fighter will certainly not save his life,
and the archer will certainly not stand, the swift of foot will certainly not be saved, nor will the horseman save his life,

relationship: same-chapter question and answer identifying the rising river
rationale: The question asks who rises like a river and churns water. The following unit explicitly answers with Egypt's rising waters and its boast of covering the land, giving the particular identification of the image.
source_text: Who is this who will rise like a river, and like rivers churn water?

target_units.text: Egypt’s waters will rise like a river, and it said, I will rise and cover the land and destroy those living in it.

relationship: parallel imperial advance pictured as rising river water
rationale: Egypt boasts of rising like a river and covering the land. Isaiah identifies strong river water with Assyria's king and describes his encampment filling the country's breadth; the invading powers differ while the military water image corresponds.
source_text: Egypt’s waters will rise like a river, and it said, I will rise and cover the land and destroy those living in it.

target_units.text: therefore, behold, the Lord brings up against you the river’s strong and abundant water—the king of the Assyrians and his glory. He will ascend every ravine of yours and walk over every wall of yours,
and he will remove from Judea a person able to lift a head or someone strong enough to accomplish anything. His encampment will fill the breadth of your country. God is with us.”

relationship: parallel Ethiopian and Libyan military contingents
rationale: Jeremiah summons Ethiopian and Libyan warriors equipped with weapons, alongside Lydian bowmen. Ezekiel likewise names Ethiopians and Libyans among an armed force, with helmets and shields, without repeating the Lydian contingent.
source_text: Mount the horses; prepare the chariots! Go out, warriors of the Ethiopians and Libyans equipped with weapons! And Lydians, go up and draw the bow!

target_units.text: Persians, Ethiopians and Libyans, all with helmets and small shields;

relationship: parallel divine sword, blood and sacrificial judgment
rationale: Jeremiah describes the Lord's day of vengeance, a sword filled and drunk with blood, and His sacrifice beside the Euphrates. Isaiah similarly joins the Lord's blood-filled sword, sacrifice in Idumea and a day of judgment and repayment.
source_text: That day belongs to the Lord our God, a day of vengeance, to take vengeance on His enemies. The Lord’s sword will devour, be filled, and become drunk with their blood, for the Lord Sabaoth has a sacrifice from the northern land beside the Euphrates River.

target_units.text: My sword became drunk in heaven. Behold, it will descend upon Idumea and upon the people of destruction, with judgment.
The Lord’s sword was filled with blood, thickened with lambs’ fat and the fat of male goats and rams, for the Lord has a sacrifice in Bosor and a great slaughter in Idumea.
The stout ones will fall with them, and rams and bulls; the earth will become drunk with blood and be filled with their fat.
For it is the Lord’s day of judgment and a year of repayment for Zion’s judgment.

relationship: parallel Gilead resin and failed national healing
rationale: Jeremiah calls on Gilead to take resin for Egypt, whose multiplied remedies are futile. Jeremiah 8 likewise names Gilead's resin and asks why healing has not risen for the people's daughter, connecting medicinal imagery with an afflicted community.
source_text: Go up, Gilead, and take resin for the virgin daughter Egypt. In vain you multiplied your remedies; there is no benefit for you.

target_units.text: Is there no resin in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why did healing not rise for the daughter of My people?

relationship: related collective collapse associated with Egyptian strength
rationale: Jeremiah describes warrior weakening against warrior and both falling together. Isaiah calls Egyptian help human and fleshly, then says the helpers grow weary and all perish together; both passages depict collective failure of relied-upon strength.
source_text: Nations heard your voice, and the land was filled with your cry, for warrior grew weak against warrior; both fell together.

target_units.text: an Egyptian human being and not God, horses’ flesh, with no help. The Lord will bring His hand against them; the helpers will grow weary, and all will perish together.

relationship: parallel announcement of Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Egypt
rationale: Both explicitly name Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as the agent of Egypt's destruction. Ezekiel expands the announcement with his people drawing swords and the land filling with wounded men.
source_text: What the Lord spoke through Jeremiah concerning Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon coming to cut down Egypt’s land:

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: I will destroy the multitude of Egyptians by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon,
him and his people: scourges from nations sent to destroy the land. They will all draw their swords against Egypt, and the land will be filled with wounded men.

relationship: related judgment announcements naming Memphis
rationale: Jeremiah commands warnings to Migdol and Memphis as the sword devours. Ezekiel likewise names Memphis in announcements of the removal of its magnates and destruction of its multitude; the target does not repeat the smilax image.
source_text: Announce to Migdol and proclaim to Memphis. Say, Take your position and prepare, for the sword has devoured your smilax growth.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: I will destroy the magnates from Memphis and the rulers from the land of Egypt, and they will be no more.
I will destroy the land of Pathros, put fire upon Tanis, and execute vengeance in Diospolis,
and pour out My wrath upon Sais, Egypt’s strength, and destroy the multitude of Memphis.

relationship: related humiliation of Egypt's named calf and handmade objects
rationale: Jeremiah asks why Apis fled and says the Lord disabled the choice calf. Isaiah likewise announces the Lord's arrival in Egypt and the shaking of Egypt's handmade objects before Him, without naming Apis individually.
source_text: Why did Apis flee? Your choice calf did not remain, for the Lord disabled him.

target_units.text: A vision of Egypt. Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and will come into Egypt; Egypt’s handmade objects will be shaken before Him, and their heart overcome within them.

relationship: repeated return to one's homeland before the Greek sword
rationale: Both passages describe people returning to their own people and land before the Greek sword. Jeremiah 26 places the speech among Egypt's weakened multitude, whereas Jeremiah 27 places the flight in the judgment upon Babylon.
source_text: Your multitude grew weak and fell, and each spoke to his neighbor, Let us rise and return to our people, to our homeland, away from the Greek sword.

target_units.text: Destroy seed from Babylon, the one holding a sickle at harvest. Before the Greek sword, each will return to his people and flee to his land.

relationship: parallel preparation of belongings for deportation
rationale: The resident daughter Egypt is commanded to prepare belongings for deportation. Ezekiel receives the same concrete instruction concerning belongings for captivity and must enact departure before his audience; the addressees and settings differ.
source_text: Prepare belongings for deportation, resident daughter Egypt, for Memphis will become a ruin and will be called Woe because no inhabitants remain in her.

target_units.text: And you, son of man, get your belongings ready for captivity by day before them. You will be taken captive from your place to another place before them, so that they may see, because they are an embittering house.
You will bring your belongings out like belongings for captivity by day before their eyes, and you yourself will go out in the evening as a captive goes out.

relationship: parallel heifer imagery for a people facing divine action
rationale: Egypt is pictured as a beautified heifer facing a northern detachment. Hosea likewise pictures Ephraim as a heifer and speaks of God coming upon the finest part of her neck, using bovine imagery for a people subject to His intervention.
source_text: Egypt is a beautified heifer; a detachment from the north came against her.

target_units.text: Ephraim is a heifer trained to love strife, but I will come upon the finest part of her neck. I will mount Ephraim and pass over Judah in silence; Jacob will strengthen him.

relationship: shared cattle imagery for threatening human forces
rationale: Egypt's hired men are likened to fed, fattened calves before their flight. The psalm likewise pictures surrounding adversaries as calves and fat bulls; it conveys their threatening presence rather than Jeremiah's subsequent collapse.
source_text: Her hired men within her are like fattened calves being fed within her. They too turned and fled together; they did not stand, for a day of destruction came upon them, the time of their vengeance.

target_units.text: Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls encompassed me.

relationship: parallel attackers with axes likened to forest cutters
rationale: Jeremiah describes attackers approaching Egypt with axes like woodcutters. The psalm describes enemies cutting doors with axes as in a forest of trees before burning the sanctuary, a particular counterpart to the cutting image in another setting.
source_text: A sound like a hissing snake, for they will travel through sand; with axes they will come against her like woodcutters.

target_units.text: As though into the entrance above,
as in a forest of trees, with axes they cut out her doors; together with axe and stone-cutting tool they tore her down.
They burned Thy sanctuary with fire; they profaned the tent of Thy name to the ground.

relationship: shared locust comparison and innumerability in accounts of invasion
rationale: Jeremiah's account of the forest being cut down combines a locust-swarm comparison with inability to number the multitude. Judges similarly describes Midian's destructive arrivals as locusts in multitude, with people and camels beyond numbering.
source_text: They will cut down her forest, says the Lord God, for it certainly cannot be estimated, for it multiplies beyond a locust swarm, and they are beyond numbering.

target_units.text: For they and their livestock came up, bringing their tents; they arrived like locusts in multitude. They and their camels were beyond numbering, and they entered Israel’s land to ruin it.

relationship: parallel captivity portrayed as Egypt's shame
rationale: Jeremiah's daughter Egypt is ashamed and handed to a northern people. Isaiah likewise describes Egypt's captivity as its shame, explicitly naming Assyria's king rather than the Babylonian setting of Jeremiah's oracle.
source_text: Daughter Egypt was put to shame, handed over to a people from the north.

target_units.text: for thus the king of the Assyrians will lead Egypt’s and the Ethiopians’ captivity, young men and elders, naked and without sandals, exposed as Egypt’s shame.

relationship: related judgment upon confidence in Pharaoh
rationale: Jeremiah announces vengeance upon Pharaoh and those trusting him. Isaiah condemns seeking Pharaoh's help and says his shelter will become shame, supplying a particular counterpart to reliance on Egypt's ruler.
source_text: I am taking vengeance for Amon her son upon Pharaoh and those who trust him.

target_units.text: you who go down to Egypt, but they did not ask Me, to be helped by Pharaoh and sheltered by Egyptians.
For Pharaoh’s shelter will become your shame, and reproach for those trusting in Egypt.

relationship: parallel rescue and gathering of Jacob from distant captivity
rationale: Jeremiah 26 promises Jacob rescue from afar, return and security. Jeremiah 38 likewise promises gathering from the north and earth's end and says the Lord ransomed Jacob from stronger hands, connecting return with divine rescue.
source_text: But do not fear, My slave Jacob, nor be terrified, Israel, for I am saving you from afar and your offspring from their captivity. Jacob will return, be quiet, and sleep, and no one will trouble him.

target_units.text: Behold, I am bringing them from the north and will gather them from the earth’s farthest end at the Passover festival. You will bear a great crowd, and they will return here.

They went out with weeping, and with encouragement I will bring them up, lodging them beside water channels on a straight road where they will certainly not wander, because I became Israel’s father, and Ephraim is My firstborn.
Hear the Lord’s word, nations, and announce it to the farther islands. Say: He who winnowed Israel will gather him and guard him like one tending his flock.
Because the Lord ransomed Jacob and rescued him from the hand of those stronger than he.

relationship: parallel refusal to destroy Jacob completely amid judgment
rationale: Jeremiah promises not to make Jacob perish while still disciplining him and refusing acquittal. Amos similarly distinguishes removal of a sinful kingdom from complete removal of Jacob's house, while retaining sword judgment upon its sinners.
source_text: Do not fear, My servant Jacob, says the Lord, for I am with you. I will make an end of every nation where I thrust you out, but I certainly will not make you perish. I will discipline you for judgment and certainly will not acquit you.

target_units.text: Look, the Lord God’s eyes are upon the kingdom of sinners, and I will remove it from the earth’s surface. Yet I will not completely remove Jacob’s house,” says the Lord.
“For look, I am giving a command: I will winnow Israel’s house among all the nations as one winnows in a winnowing basket, and no fragment will fall to the ground.
All the sinners of My people will die by a sword, those who say, ‘Evils certainly will not draw near or come upon us.’

relationship: parallel humiliation of Bel and powerless images
rationale: Jeremiah announces Babylon's capture and Bel's disgrace alongside Marodach's surrender. Isaiah likewise names Bel's fall and depicts carved images as burdens carried into captivity; its other named figure is Dagon, not Marodach.
source_text: Announce among the nations and make it heard; do not hide it. Say, Babylon has been captured! Bel was disgraced, the fearless one; the delicate one was handed over, Marodach.

target_units.text: Bel fell; Dagon was shattered. Their carved images became a burden for wild and domestic animals. Lift them, bound together, as a load for one who is weary
and hungry and exhausted, without strength at all; they cannot be saved from war, and they themselves were led captive.

relationship: parallel conquest leaving Babylon uninhabited
rationale: Jeremiah announces a northern nation making Babylon's land a ruin without inhabitants. Isaiah names the Medes and likewise predicts Babylon's overthrow and enduring lack of habitation, without specifying the northern direction in this passage.
source_text: A nation came up against her from the north; it will make her land a ruin, with no one living in it, from human to livestock.

target_units.text: Behold, I am rousing the Medes against you, who do not value silver or have need of gold.
They will shatter young men’s arrows and certainly not pity your children; their eyes will not spare the children.
Babylon, which is called glorious by the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.
She will not be inhabited for everlasting time, nor will people ever enter her through many generations. Arabs will certainly not pass through her, and shepherds will certainly not rest in her.

relationship: parallel joint return of Israel and Judah
rationale: Jeremiah 27 pictures Israel's and Judah's sons coming together to seek God. Jeremiah 3 likewise promises that Judah will join Israel and together return to the ancestral land, a particular reunion of the two houses.
source_text: In those days and at that time, Israel’s sons and Judah’s sons will come together; walking and weeping, they will go seeking the Lord their God.

target_units.text: In those days the house of Judah will join the house of Israel, and together they will come from the northern land and from all the regions to the land I gave their fathers as an inheritance.

relationship: parallel everlasting covenant and language of refuge
rationale: The returning people turn toward Zion and take refuge with God under an everlasting covenant. Isaiah likewise promises an everlasting covenant, specifies David's sure blessings and describes peoples fleeing to the addressee for refuge because of Israel's God.
source_text: They will ask the way as far as Zion, for they will turn their faces here. They will come and take refuge with the Lord God, for an everlasting covenant will not be forgotten.

target_units.text: Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.
Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a ruler and commander of nations.
Nations that did not know you will call upon you, and peoples that do not know you will flee to you for refuge, because of your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you.

relationship: parallel lost sheep scattered through failed shepherding
rationale: Jeremiah's people are lost sheep driven astray by shepherds across mountains and hills. Ezekiel likewise charges shepherds with failing to recover the lost and describes God's sheep scattered over mountains and high hills.
source_text: My people became lost sheep; their shepherds thrust them away and led them astray upon the mountains. They went from mountain to hill and forgot their resting place.

target_units.text: You have not strengthened the weak, restored the sick to health, bound up the broken, brought back the wandering or sought the lost. You have worn down the strong with toil.
My sheep scattered because there were no shepherds and became food for all the field’s beasts.
My sheep scattered on every mountain and upon every high hill, and scattered over the whole face of the earth. There was no one seeking them out or turning them back.

relationship: parallel captors attributing calamity to disobedience against the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah 27 reports enemies holding the people because they sinned against the Lord. The chief guard in Jeremiah 47 similarly attributes the calamities to sin and refusal to obey God; neither comparison requires the enemies' conduct to be vindicated.
source_text: All who found them consumed them. Their enemies said, Let us not release them, because they sinned against the Lord, the pasture of righteousness, who gathered their fathers.

target_units.text: The chief guard took him and said to him, The Lord your God spoke these calamities against this place.
And the Lord acted, because you sinned against Him and did not obey His voice.

relationship: parallel command to leave Babylon and the Chaldeans
rationale: Both explicitly command departure from Babylon and the Chaldeans. Isaiah adds public proclamation of Jacob's rescue; it does not repeat Jeremiah's unusual comparison with dragons before sheep.
source_text: Separate yourselves from Babylon’s midst and the Chaldeans’ land; come out and become like dragons before sheep.

target_units.text: Leave Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans. Announce a voice of rejoicing, and let this be heard; proclaim it to the earth’s extremity. Say, “The Lord rescued His slave Jacob.”

relationship: parallel divine mustering of nations against Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah announces God rousing assembled nations against Babylon. Isaiah's Babylon vision likewise describes kings and gathered nations with the Lord's armed fighters coming from afar; Jeremiah additionally specifies the north and a successful missile.
source_text: I am rousing assemblies of nations against Babylon from the north. They will deploy against her; from there she will be captured. Like a discerning warrior’s missile, it will not return empty.

target_units.text: A sound of many nations upon the mountains, like many nations; a sound of kings and gathered nations. The Lord Sabaoth has commanded an armed nation,
to come from a distant land, from the farthest edge of heaven’s foundation—the Lord and His armed fighters—to destroy the whole inhabited world.

relationship: parallel reversal in which plunderers become plunder
rationale: Chaldea becomes plunder, with its plunderers filled, following its attacks upon God's inheritance. Habakkuk likewise says the one who despoiled many nations will become plunder for the remaining peoples.
source_text: Chaldea will become plunder; all who plunder her will be filled.

target_units.text: For suddenly those biting him will rise, and those plotting against you will awake; you will become their plunder.
Because you despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of human bloodshed and impiety against land, city and all its inhabitants.

relationship: parallel condemnation of rejoicing over Judah's devastation
rationale: Jeremiah condemns Babylon's rejoicing and boasting while plundering God's inheritance. Obadiah likewise forbids rejoicing and boasting over Judah's destruction and joining the attack, addressing a different hostile neighbor.
source_text: because you rejoiced and boasted while plundering My inheritance, because you leaped like little cattle in pasture and butted like bulls,

target_units.text: From the day you stood opposed, on the day foreigners took his strength captive and strangers entered his gates and cast lots over Jerusalem, you too were like one of them.
Do not look on your brother’s day, on the day of strangers; do not rejoice over the sons of Judah on the day of their destruction; do not speak boastfully on the day of affliction.

Do not enter the gates of peoples on the day of their suffering. You, too, must not look on their assembly on the day of their destruction, and do not join in attacking their strength on the day of their destruction.

relationship: parallel shame and lowered status for personified Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah depicts Babylon's mother deeply ashamed and last among nations. Isaiah similarly addresses daughter Babylon, commands her descent and announces exposed shame and loss of her title as a kingdom's strength.
source_text: your mother was deeply ashamed—a mother for good things, last of nations, a wilderness.

target_units.text: “Come down and sit on the ground, virgin daughter Babylon. Enter darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, for you will no longer be called tender and pampered.
Take a millstone and grind flour. Uncover your veil, expose your gray hair, pull up your garments to bare your lower legs, and cross rivers.
Your shame will be uncovered, and your reproaches will be visible. I will exact justice from you; I will certainly no longer hand it over to humans.”
The One who rescued you said—His name is the Lord Sabaoth, Israel’s Holy One—
“Sit stricken and enter darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans. You will certainly no longer be called a kingdom’s strength.

relationship: parallel lasting desolation of Babylon
rationale: Both explicitly name Babylon and deny her continuing habitation after divine judgment. Isaiah develops the replacement of human habitation with wild and uncanny creatures, whereas Jeremiah emphasizes passersby's reaction to her wounds.
source_text: Because of the Lord’s anger she will not be inhabited and will entirely disappear. Everyone passing through Babylon will look gloomy, and they will hiss at every wound of hers.

target_units.text: Babylon, which is called glorious by the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.
She will not be inhabited for everlasting time, nor will people ever enter her through many generations. Arabs will certainly not pass through her, and shepherds will certainly not rest in her.
Wild beasts will rest there, and the houses fill with sound; sirens will rest there, and demons dance there.
Donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs make nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay.

relationship: parallel commands to deploy archers against Babylon
rationale: Both passages command drawing bows against Babylon. Jeremiah 27 says not to spare arrows, while Jeremiah 28 says not to spare her young men and to obliterate her force; the objects of those commands remain distinct.
source_text: Deploy against Babylon all around, all who stretch the bow. Shoot at her; do not spare your arrows.

target_units.text: Against her let the archer stretch his bow, and let the man who has armor put it on. Do not spare her young men; obliterate her whole force.

relationship: parallel repayment of Babylon according to her own acts
rationale: Jeremiah calls for vengeance upon Babylon, doing to her what she did. The psalm likewise addresses daughter Babylon and describes repayment of the repayment she gave the speakers, expressing the same retaliatory measure.
source_text: Clap against her! Her hands were disabled, her battlements fell, and her wall was demolished. For this is vengeance from God; take vengeance upon her. Do to her as she did.

target_units.text: Daughter Babylon, miserable one, happy is the one who will repay you the repayment you gave us.

relationship: repeated return to one's people before the Greek sword
rationale: Jeremiah 27 joins the destruction of Babylon's agriculture with people returning to their own land before the Greek sword. Jeremiah 26 gives the same homeland-return language in the speech of Egypt's weakened multitude.
source_text: Destroy seed from Babylon, the one holding a sickle at harvest. Before the Greek sword, each will return to his people and flee to his land.

target_units.text: Your multitude grew weak and fell, and each spoke to his neighbor, Let us rise and return to our people, to our homeland, away from the Greek sword.

relationship: historical counterpart to the Assyrian attack pictured as devouring
rationale: Jeremiah names Assyria's king as the first lion to consume wandering Israel. Kings records the Assyrian siege and capture of Samaria and Israel's deportation, giving the historical action corresponding to that first named attacker.
source_text: Israel is a wandering sheep driven away by lions. First Assyria’s king ate him; later this one, Babylon’s king, ate his bones.

target_units.text: The king of the Assyrians went up through the whole land, went up to Samaria, and besieged it for three years.
In Hoshea’s ninth year the king of the Assyrians captured Samaria and deported Israel to the Assyrians. He settled them in Alae and Abor, rivers of Gozan, and Ore of the Medes.

relationship: historical counterpart to the later Babylonian attack
rationale: Jeremiah names Babylon's king as the later devourer after Assyria. Kings records Babylon's siege of Jerusalem and deportation of its rulers and powerful people, corresponding to the second imperial attacker without reproducing the bone-eating image.
source_text: Israel is a wandering sheep driven away by lions. First Assyria’s king ate him; later this one, Babylon’s king, ate his bones.

target_units.text: At that time Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon came up to Jerusalem, and the city came under siege.
Nabouchodonosor king of Babylon entered the city while his servants were besieging it.
Joakim king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, he, his servants, his mother, his rulers, and his eunuchs. The king of Babylon took him in the eighth year of his reign.

He brought out from there all the treasures of the Lord’s house and the treasures of the king’s house. He cut apart all the gold vessels Solomon king of Israel had made in the Lord’s sanctuary, according to the Lord’s word.
He deported Jerusalem, all the rulers, and the mighty in strength, taking ten thousand captives, and every craftsman and one who shuts up. None remained except the land’s poor.
He deported Joakim to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, and his eunuchs. He led the land’s powerful men into deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon,
and all the men of the force, seven thousand, and the craftsmen and those who shut up, one thousand—all mighty men who waged war. The king of Babylon brought them into deportation to Babylon.

relationship: related announcement of punishment upon Assyria's king
rationale: Jeremiah promises punishment upon Babylon's king like the punishment upon Assyria's king. Isaiah supplies a particular prophetic announcement of judgment upon Assyria's ruler after the Lord's work in Zion and Jerusalem.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: I am taking vengeance upon Babylon’s king and his land, as I took vengeance upon Assyria’s king.

target_units.text: When the Lord has finished doing all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, He will bring judgment upon the great mind—the ruler of the Assyrians—and upon the height of the glory of his eyes.

relationship: parallel restoration of Israel's pasture in named regions
rationale: Jeremiah promises Israel restored grazing on Carmel and in Gilead, also naming Ephraim. Micah likewise describes the sheep of God's inheritance in Carmel and grazing in Gilead, while additionally naming Bashan.
source_text: I will restore Israel to his pasture. He will graze on Carmel, on Ephraim’s mountain, and in Gilead, and his soul will be filled.

target_units.text: Shepherd Thy people with Thy rod, the sheep of Thine inheritance, camping by themselves in a forest amid Carmel. They will graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old.

relationship: parallel mercy removing the remnant's sins
rationale: Jeremiah says Israel's and Judah's sins will not be found because God will show mercy to those remaining. Micah likewise joins the remaining inheritance, God's desire for mercy and the removal of injustices, picturing sins cast into the sea.
source_text: In those days and at that time they will seek Israel’s injustice, and it will not exist, and Judah’s sins, and they certainly will not be found, for I will be merciful to those left upon the land, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Who is a God like Thee, removing injustices and passing over impieties for the remaining ones of His inheritance? He did not retain His anger as a testimony, because He desires mercy.
He Himself will turn back and pity us; He will sink our injustices, and they will be thrown into the depths of the sea—all our sins.

relationship: parallel sword judgment carried out by divine command
rationale: Jeremiah commands the sword to take vengeance and do what the Lord orders. Jeremiah 29 likewise explains that the Lord's sword cannot be quiet because He commanded its action against coastal places; the threatened territories differ.
source_text: Go fiercely against her and her inhabitants. Take vengeance, sword, and make her disappear, says the Lord; do everything I command you.

target_units.text: sword of the Lord? How long will you not be quiet? Return to your sheath; rest and be lifted away!
How will it be quiet? The Lord commanded it to rise against Ashkelon, against the coastal places, against those remaining.

relationship: repeated sound of great shattering in the Chaldeans' land
rationale: Both passages locate a sound and great shattering in the Chaldeans' land. Jeremiah 27 names the sound of war, while Jeremiah 28 names crying in Babylon, closely corresponding descriptions of the city's calamity.
source_text: A sound of war and great shattering in the Chaldeans’ land!

target_units.text: A sound of crying in Babylon, a great shattering in the Chaldeans’ land!

relationship: parallel breaking of Babylon's instrument of domination
rationale: Jeremiah calls Babylon the shattered hammer of the whole earth. Isaiah's lament against Babylon's king says God shattered the rulers' yoke; the tools differ while both images portray broken imperial domination.
source_text: How the hammer of the whole earth was snapped and shattered! How Babylon became a ruin among nations!

target_units.text: and you will take up this lament against Babylon’s king and say on that day, “How the one who made demands has rested, and the taskmaster rested!
God shattered the sinners’ yoke, the rulers’ yoke;

relationship: parallel destruction overtaking Babylon without her knowing
rationale: Jeremiah announces Babylon's capture without her knowledge because she resisted the Lord. Isaiah likewise confronts confident daughter Babylon and repeats that sudden destruction will come without her knowing it.
source_text: They will attack you and you will be captured, Babylon, without knowing it. You were found and taken because you resisted the Lord.

target_units.text: in your hope of wickedness. For you said, ‘I am, and there is no other.’ Know that understanding these things and your prostitution will become your shame. You said in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no other.’

Destruction will come upon you, and you will certainly not know it—a pit, and you will fall into it. Misery will come upon you, and you will certainly not be able to become clean. Destruction will come upon you suddenly, and you will certainly not know it.

relationship: parallel divine forces deployed in the Babylon judgment
rationale: Jeremiah depicts God bringing instruments of His anger from a treasury for work in Chaldea. Isaiah's Babylon vision likewise describes forces led to fulfill divine wrath and the Lord's armed fighters coming for destruction, without the treasury detail.
source_text: The Lord opened His treasury and brought out the instruments of His anger, for the Lord God has work in the Chaldeans’ land,

target_units.text: I command, and I lead them; they are consecrated, and I lead them. Giants are coming to fulfill My wrath, rejoicing and acting insolently together.
A sound of many nations upon the mountains, like many nations; a sound of kings and gathered nations. The Lord Sabaoth has commanded an armed nation,
to come from a distant land, from the farthest edge of heaven’s foundation—the Lord and His armed fighters—to destroy the whole inhabited world.

relationship: parallel removal of Babylon's remnant
rationale: The order to open Babylon's storehouses and destroy her concludes that no remnant should remain. Isaiah likewise announces the destruction of her name, remnant and offspring and the desolation of Babylonia; it does not repeat the cave-search image.
source_text: for her times have arrived. Open her storehouses; search her like a cave and destroy her. Let no remnant of her remain.

target_units.text: “I will rise against them,” says the Lord Sabaoth, “and destroy their name, remnant and offspring”—thus says the Lord—
“and make Babylonia deserted, so that hedgehogs dwell there; she will become nothing. I will make her a muddy abyss for destruction.”

relationship: parallel departure from Babylon accompanied by proclamation
rationale: Jeremiah pictures escapees from Babylon announcing the Lord's vengeance in Zion. Isaiah likewise joins departure from Babylon with public announcement of the Lord's rescue of Jacob, presenting the complementary rescue side of the judgment.
source_text: A sound of those fleeing and being rescued from Babylon’s land, announcing in Zion vengeance from the Lord our God!

target_units.text: Leave Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans. Announce a voice of rejoicing, and let this be heard; proclaim it to the earth’s extremity. Say, “The Lord rescued His slave Jacob.”

relationship: parallel recompense according to prior conduct
rationale: Jeremiah orders repayment of Babylon according to her works, doing to her what she did. Obadiah similarly says that as the addressed enemy acted, so it will happen to him, with recompense returned upon his own head.
source_text: Give orders against Babylon to many, to everyone drawing a bow. Encamp against her all around; let none of her people escape. Repay her according to her works; do to her all she did, for she resisted the Lord, Israel’s holy God.

target_units.text: For the day of the Lord is near against all the nations. Just as you acted, so it will be for you; your recompense will be repaid upon your own head.

relationship: repeated fall of young men in squares and warriors
rationale: Both judgments announce young men falling in public squares and the fall of warriors. Jeremiah 27 addresses Babylon, while Jeremiah 30 places the corresponding announcement in the Damascus oracle.
source_text: Therefore her young men will fall in her squares, and all her warriors will be thrown down, said the Lord.

target_units.text: Therefore young men will fall in your squares, and all your warriors will fall, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel judgment upon confident personified Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah addresses Babylon as an insolent woman whose day of vengeance has arrived. Isaiah likewise addresses her confident claim to lasting rule and announces sudden loss and destruction, exposing the failure of that confidence.
source_text: I am against you, insolent woman, says the Lord, for your day has come, the time of your vengeance.

target_units.text: You said, ‘I will rule for ever.’ You did not consider these things in your heart or remember the last things.
Now hear these things, pampered one who sits confident, saying in her heart, ‘I am, and there is no other. I will not sit as a widow or know bereavement.’
Now these two will come upon you suddenly, in one day: widowhood and childlessness will come suddenly upon you, amid your sorcery and the overwhelming power of your enchanters,

in your hope of wickedness. For you said, ‘I am, and there is no other.’ Know that understanding these things and your prostitution will become your shame. You said in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no other.’

Destruction will come upon you, and you will certainly not know it—a pit, and you will fall into it. Misery will come upon you, and you will certainly not be able to become clean. Destruction will come upon you suddenly, and you will certainly not know it.

relationship: parallel insolence preceding ruin and a fall
rationale: Jeremiah says Babylon's insolence will weaken and fall without anyone raising it. Proverbs states the corresponding moral pattern: insolence goes before ruin and evil-mindedness before a fall; it does not supply the forest-fire detail.
source_text: Your insolence will grow weak and fall, with no one to raise it. I will kindle fire in her forest, and it will devour everything around her.

target_units.text: Insolence leads before ruin, and evil-mindedness before a fall.

relationship: parallel oppression joined with refusal to release Israel
rationale: Jeremiah's captors oppress Israel and Judah and refuse their release. Pharaoh likewise refuses to let Israel go and increases the people's labor, supplying a particular earlier pattern of captivity, oppression and rejected release.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Israel’s sons and Judah’s sons have been oppressed together. All who captured them oppressed them, because they did not want to release them.

target_units.text: Afterward Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said, “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: ‘Let My people go so that they may hold a feast for Me in the wilderness.’”
Pharaoh said, “Who is He, that I should obey His voice and let the sons of Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go.”
They said to him, “The God of the Hebrews has called us. We will go a three days’ journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to our God, lest death or slaughter meet us.”
And the king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why do you turn my people from their works? Each of you, go back to your work.”
And Pharaoh said, “Behold, the people are now numerous; let us not therefore give them rest from their works.”
Pharaoh commanded the people’s taskmasters and scribes:
“The people shall no longer be given straw for making bricks as before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.

And you shall lay upon them the appointed number of bricks which they make each day; you shall not reduce it at all. For they are idle; therefore they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
Let these men’s tasks be heavier. Let them attend to them and pay no attention to empty words.”

relationship: parallel mighty redeemer judging a case
rationale: Jeremiah calls the people's redeemer strong and says He will judge a case against adversaries. Proverbs likewise calls the orphans' redeeming Lord mighty and says He will judge their case, applying the same protective legal image to a different vulnerable group.
source_text: The One redeeming them is strong; the Lord Almighty is His name. He will judge a case against His adversaries, to remove the land, and He will provoke Babylon’s inhabitants.

target_units.text: Do not move everlasting boundaries, and do not enter orphans’ property,
for the Lord who redeems them is mighty, and He will judge their case with you.

relationship: parallel judgment reaching Babylon's leaders and wise men
rationale: Jeremiah 27 directs sword judgment against Babylon's inhabitants, nobles and discerning men. Jeremiah 28 likewise names leaders, wise men and generals as recipients of divine judgment, there expressed as thorough intoxication.
source_text: A sword against the Chaldeans, Babylon’s inhabitants, her nobles, and her discerning men!

target_units.text: He will make her leaders and wise men and generals thoroughly drunk, says the King, whose name is the Lord Almighty.

relationship: parallel disabling of Babylon's warriors
rationale: Jeremiah announces a sword against the warriors and their disabling. Jeremiah 28 describes Babylon's warrior ceasing to fight and the crushing of their power, a concrete counterpart to the loss of military ability.
source_text: A sword against her warriors, and they will be disabled!

target_units.text: Babylon’s warrior has ceased fighting; they will sit there in confinement. Their power was crushed; they became like women. Her dwellings were burned; her bars were shattered.

relationship: shared image of a city's defenders becoming like women
rationale: Jeremiah describes Babylon's warriors and mixed population becoming like women amid sword judgment. Nahum uses the same gendered image for the people within the threatened city as its gates open to enemies; the comparison concerns the texts' portrayal of failed defense.
source_text: A sword against their horses and chariots! A sword against their warriors and the mixed people within her, and they will become like women! A sword against her treasures, and they will be scattered!

target_units.text: Look, your people within you are like women! The gates of your land will open wide to your enemies, and fire will consume your bars.

relationship: related contrast between confidence in water and its threatened drying
rationale: Babylon trusted in her water but will be ashamed. Jeremiah 28 announces that God will lay her sea waste and dry her spring, providing a particular judgment against the water associated with that confidence.
source_text: She trusted in her water, and they will be ashamed, for it is a land of carved images, and in the islands where they boasted.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord: I will judge your adversary and avenge you; I will lay her sea waste and dry her spring.

relationship: parallel uncanny inhabitants replacing human habitation in Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah places apparitions on the islands and daughters of sirens in Babylon, while denying future habitation. Isaiah likewise denies Babylon human habitation and places sirens and other uncanny creatures there, without reproducing Jeremiah's island clause.
source_text: Therefore apparitions will live on the islands, and daughters of sirens will live in her. She certainly will never again be inhabited.

target_units.text: She will not be inhabited for everlasting time, nor will people ever enter her through many generations. Arabs will certainly not pass through her, and shepherds will certainly not rest in her.
Wild beasts will rest there, and the houses fill with sound; sirens will rest there, and demons dance there.
Donkey-centaurs will dwell there, and hedgehogs make nests in their houses. It comes quickly and will not delay.

relationship: explicit comparison with the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah
rationale: Jeremiah expressly compares Babylon's desolation with God's overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah and bordering places. Genesis narrates that overthrow of the cities and surrounding country, supplying the named event used in the comparison.
source_text: As God overturned Sodom, Gomorrah, and their bordering places, said the Lord, no person will live there, and no human being will reside there.

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: repeated northern people and nations from the earth's extremity
rationale: Both passages announce a people coming from the north and a force roused from the earth's farthest part. Jeremiah 27 applies the pattern to Babylon and additionally names many kings; Jeremiah 6 introduces the attack on Zion.
source_text: A people is coming from the north; a great nation and many kings will be roused from the earth’s farthest part,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people comes from the north, and nations will be roused from the earth’s extremity.

relationship: parallel merciless mounted force with a sea-like voice
rationale: Both describe armed riders who show no mercy, whose voice resembles the sea and who prepare like fire for war. Jeremiah 27 addresses daughter Babylon, whereas Jeremiah 6 addresses daughter Zion and additionally names chariots.
source_text: holding bow and dagger. It is insolent and certainly will not show mercy. Their voice will sound like the sea. They will ride horses, prepared like fire for war against you, daughter Babylon.

target_units.text: They will grasp bow and spear; it is ruthless and will show no mercy. Its voice is like a surging sea; on horses and chariots it will draw up like fire for war against you, daughter of Zion.

relationship: repeated report, disabled hands and birth-pain distress
rationale: Babylon's king hears the report, loses strength in his hands and is seized by birth-pain distress. Jeremiah 6 uses the same sequence in the people's first-person report of the force threatening Zion.
source_text: Babylon’s king heard the report about them, and his hands were disabled. Distress seized him, birth pains like a woman giving birth.

target_units.text: We heard the report of them; our hands were paralyzed. Affliction seized us, labor pains like a woman giving birth.

relationship: repeated lion, Jordan and incomparable divine power imagery
rationale: Both passages describe a lion coming from the Jordan into Aitham's place and ask who can resist God or what shepherd can stand before Him. The corresponding images occur in Babylon's and Idumea's distinct judgment oracles.
source_text: Like a lion he will come up from the Jordan into Aitham’s place, for I will quickly drive them away from her and appoint every young man over her. For who is like Me? Who will resist Me, and what shepherd can stand before Me?

target_units.text: Like a lion he will come up from Jordan’s midst into Aitham’s place, for I will quickly drive them away from her. Appoint the young men over her. For who is like Me? Who will resist Me, and what shepherd can stand before Me?

relationship: parallel divine counsel expressed through sheep and pasture
rationale: Jeremiah announces God's counsel against Babylon and consequences for lambs and pasture. The Idumea oracle likewise announces God's counsel and purposes, followed by small sheep and a dwelling made untrodden; the locations and exact outcomes differ.
source_text: Therefore hear the Lord’s counsel that He has planned against Babylon and His purposes against the resident Chaldeans: Surely the lambs of their sheep will be destroyed; surely pasture will disappear from them.

target_units.text: Therefore hear the Lord’s counsel that He planned against Idumea and His purpose against Teman’s inhabitants: Surely the smallest sheep will be swept together; surely their dwelling will be made untrodden over her.

relationship: parallel earth-shaking fall and widely heard cry
rationale: Babylon's capture shakes the earth and produces a cry among nations. The Idumea oracle similarly describes earth shaking at a fall and a cry heard at the sea, using the same coupled effects in another judgment.
source_text: For at the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will shake, and a cry will be heard among the nations.

target_units.text: For at the sound of their fall the earth shook, and your cry was heard at the sea.

relationship: parallel destructive hot wind brought by the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah announces a destroying hot wind roused against Babylon. Hosea likewise says the Lord brings a scorching wilderness wind that dries channels, springs and land, a particular weather image of destructive divine action.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: I am rousing a destroying hot wind against Babylon and against the Chaldeans who live there.

target_units.text: Because this one will make a division among brothers. The Lord will bring a scorching wind from the wilderness upon him and dry up his channels and desolate his springs; it will dry his land and all his desirable vessels.

relationship: parallel insolent forces directed against Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah says God will send insolent men to ravage Babylon. Isaiah's Babylon vision likewise describes forces led by God and giants acting insolently together to fulfill His wrath, without identifying the two groups.
source_text: I will send insolent men to Babylon; they will abuse her and ravage her land. Woe upon Babylon all around on the day of her affliction!

target_units.text: I command, and I lead them; they are consecrated, and I lead them. Giants are coming to fulfill My wrath, rejoicing and acting insolently together.

relationship: parallel orders to draw bows against Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah 28 commands the archer to draw his bow against Babylon and denies mercy to her force. Jeremiah 27 likewise commands archers to deploy and shoot at her, specifying that arrows should not be spared.
source_text: Against her let the archer stretch his bow, and let the man who has armor put it on. Do not spare her young men; obliterate her whole force.

target_units.text: Deploy against Babylon all around, all who stretch the bow. Shoot at her; do not spare your arrows.

relationship: parallel fallen fighters in Babylon's judgment
rationale: Jeremiah 28 describes wounded and pierced men falling in and outside the Chaldeans' land. Jeremiah 27 likewise announces fallen young men and warriors in Babylon's judgment, locating the young men's fall in her squares.
source_text: Wounded men will fall in the Chaldeans’ land, and pierced men outside her.

target_units.text: Therefore her young men will fall in her squares, and all her warriors will be thrown down, said the Lord.

relationship: related denial of lasting abandonment through widowhood imagery
rationale: Jeremiah says Israel and Judah have not been widowed of their God. Isaiah similarly promises the end of widowhood's reproach and speaks of God's mercy toward one compared with a wife, while retaining its own description of brief abandonment.
source_text: For Israel and Judah have not been widowed of their God, of the Lord Almighty, because their land was filled with injustice from Israel’s holy ones.

target_units.text: Do not fear because you were put to shame, or be abashed because you were reproached. For you will forget lasting shame and never remember the reproach of your widowhood.
For the Lord is the One making you; the Lord Sabaoth is His name. The One who rescued you is Himself Israel’s God; He will be called upon throughout all earth.
“The Lord has not called you like an abandoned, fainthearted wife, nor like a wife hated since youth,” says your God.
“For a short time I abandoned you, and with great mercy I will have mercy on you.
In a little anger I turned My face from you, and with everlasting mercy I will have mercy on you,” says the Lord who rescued you.

relationship: parallel command to escape Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah commands each person to flee Babylon and save life at the time of recompense. Isaiah likewise commands leaving Babylon and fleeing the Chaldeans, joining departure with the proclamation that the Lord rescued Jacob.
source_text: Flee from Babylon’s midst; each of you save your life. Do not be cast away in her injustice, for her time of vengeance is from the Lord; He is repaying her recompense.

target_units.text: Leave Babylon, fleeing from the Chaldeans. Announce a voice of rejoicing, and let this be heard; proclaim it to the earth’s extremity. Say, “The Lord rescued His slave Jacob.”

relationship: parallel cup in the Lord's hand affecting the earth
rationale: Babylon is a golden cup in the Lord's hand whose wine shakes the nations. The psalm likewise places a wine cup in the Lord's hand and says all the earth's sinners will drink, while not identifying its cup with Babylon.
source_text: Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, making the whole earth drunk. Nations drank her wine; therefore they were shaken.

target_units.text: For in the Lord’s hand is a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture; and He tilted from this into that, but its dregs were not emptied out; all the earth’s sinners will drink.

relationship: same-chapter proposed healing and its unsuccessful outcome
rationale: After Babylon's sudden fall, the text calls for resin in case she can be healed. The next unit reports that Babylon was treated but not healed, directly answering the proposed medicinal response.
source_text: Suddenly Babylon fell and was shattered. Lament her! Take resin for her corruption, if somehow she may be healed.

target_units.text: We treated Babylon, but she was not healed. Let us leave her; let each of us go to our own land, for her judgment reached heaven and rose to the stars.

relationship: parallel futile treatment of a judged nation
rationale: Jeremiah 28 reports that Babylon was treated without healing. The Egypt oracle similarly calls for Gilead's resin yet says multiplied remedies bring no benefit, extending the failed-healing image to a different nation.
source_text: We treated Babylon, but she was not healed. Let us leave her; let each of us go to our own land, for her judgment reached heaven and rose to the stars.

target_units.text: Go up, Gilead, and take resin for the virgin daughter Egypt. In vain you multiplied your remedies; there is no benefit for you.

relationship: parallel announcement of the Lord's action in Zion
rationale: Jeremiah 28 calls for announcing the Lord's works in Zion after His judgment is brought forth. Jeremiah 27 likewise pictures rescued people from Babylon announcing the Lord's vengeance in Zion.
source_text: The Lord has brought forth His judgment. Come, let us announce in Zion the works of the Lord our God.

target_units.text: A sound of those fleeing and being rescued from Babylon’s land, announcing in Zion vengeance from the Lord our God!

relationship: parallel divine rousing of the Medes against Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord roused the Medes' king for Babylon's destruction. Isaiah's Babylon oracle likewise explicitly announces God rousing the Medes, adding their disregard for wealth and lack of pity.
source_text: Prepare the arrows; fill the quivers. The Lord roused the spirit of the Medes’ king, for His anger against Babylon is to destroy her. This is the Lord’s vengeance, vengeance for His people.

target_units.text: Behold, I am rousing the Medes against you, who do not value silver or have need of gold.
They will shatter young men’s arrows and certainly not pity your children; their eyes will not spare the children.

relationship: parallel preparation against Babylon's fortifications
rationale: Jeremiah 28 commands a signal, guards and weapons at Babylon's walls as the Lord carries out His word. Jeremiah 27 likewise orders deployment around the city and announces fallen battlements and a demolished wall.
source_text: Raise a signal on Babylon’s walls; set up quivers, raise guards, prepare weapons, for the Lord has undertaken and will do what He spoke against Babylon’s inhabitants,

target_units.text: Deploy against Babylon all around, all who stretch the bow. Shoot at her; do not spare your arrows.
Clap against her! Her hands were disabled, her battlements fell, and her wall was demolished. For this is vengeance from God; take vengeance upon her. Do to her as she did.

relationship: related threat to Babylon beside the waters she trusted
rationale: Jeremiah 28 addresses Babylon beside many waters and announces her end. Jeremiah 27 says she trusted in her water and will be ashamed, connecting the watery setting with failed confidence without interpreting the inward-parts phrase.
source_text: who dwell beside many waters and her abundance of treasures. Your end has truly come to your inward parts.

target_units.text: She trusted in her water, and they will be ashamed, for it is a land of carved images, and in the islands where they boasted.

relationship: parallel divine oath by the arm
rationale: Jeremiah announces that the Lord swore by His arm before threatening Babylon. Isaiah likewise records an oath by the Lord's right hand and strong arm, there promising protection of Jerusalem's produce rather than an enemy's defeat.
source_text: For the Lord swore by His arm: I will fill you with people like locusts, and those coming down will speak out against you.

target_units.text: The Lord swore by His right hand and the strength of His arm: “I will no longer give your grain and food to your enemies, nor will foreigners drink your wine for which you toiled.

relationship: repeated creation by divine strength, wisdom and understanding
rationale: Both passages describe the earth made by God's strength, the inhabited world established through wisdom, and heaven stretched out by understanding. The closely corresponding clauses affirm the Creator in settings that also expose powerless images.
source_text: He makes the earth by His strength, prepares the inhabited world by His wisdom, and stretched out heaven by His understanding.

target_units.text: The Lord who made the earth by His strength, who set the inhabited world upright by His wisdom, also stretched out heaven by His understanding,

relationship: repeated heavenly waters, clouds, lightning and light
rationale: Both describe heavenly water, clouds brought from the earth's extremity, lightning for rain and light brought from divine treasuries. Jeremiah 28 additionally introduces the sound of water through God's voice; neither supplied unit says wind from the treasuries.
source_text: At His voice He set a sound of water in heaven and brought clouds up from the earth’s end. He made lightning for rain and brought light out of His treasuries.

target_units.text: and an abundance of water in heaven; and He brought clouds up from the earth’s extremity, made lightning for rain, and brought light out of His treasuries.

relationship: repeated shame of makers of lifeless images
rationale: Both say people become foolish without knowledge and goldsmiths are disgraced by their carved things. They explain that the cast things are false and contain no spirit, giving a close verbal counterpart to the critique.
source_text: Every person became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was disgraced by his carvings, because they cast false things, and there is no spirit in them.

target_units.text: Every human became foolish, without knowledge; every goldsmith was put to shame at his carved things, because they cast false things; there is no spirit in them.

relationship: repeated futility and destruction of manufactured images
rationale: Both call the objects vain or futile, mocked works, and predict their destruction at the time of visitation. The correspondence concerns the same verdict upon manufactured objects in the surrounding idol critiques.
source_text: They are vain, mocked works; at the time of their visitation they will perish.

target_units.text: They are futile, mocked works; at the time of their visitation they will perish.

relationship: repeated contrast between Jacob's inheritance and manufactured objects
rationale: Both deny that Jacob's portion resembles the futile images and identify the One who formed everything as his inheritance. Both conclude by naming Him Lord, distinguishing Creator from manufacture.
source_text: Jacob’s portion is not like this, for the One who formed all things is Himself his inheritance. The Lord is His name.

target_units.text: Jacob’s portion is not such as this, because the One who formed everything is himself his inheritance; Lord is His name.

relationship: related military instruments within divine judgment
rationale: Jeremiah links scattering instruments of war for God with nations scattered in the addressee and kings removed from the addressee. Isaiah's Assyrian oracle likewise joins military force, the rod of divine anger and commanded plunder, without identifying Jeremiah's unnamed addressee as Assyria.
source_text: You scatter instruments of war for Me. In you I will scatter nations, and from you I will remove kings.

target_units.text: Woe to the Assyrians! The rod of My anger and wrath is in their hands.
I will send My anger against a lawless nation, and I will command My people to take spoils and plunder, trample the cities and reduce them to dust.
But he did not consider it this way and has not reckoned it this way in his soul; rather, his mind will turn aside, even to destroy not a few nations.

relationship: parallel overthrow of horses, riders and chariots
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering of horse and rider and of chariots and their riders. Haggai similarly describes God overturning chariots and riders and horses with their riders falling, within judgment upon royal power.
source_text: In you I will scatter horse and rider; in you I will scatter chariots and their riders.

target_units.text: and I will overturn the thrones of kings and destroy the strength of the kings of the nations. I will overturn chariots and riders; horses and their riders will fall, each with a sword against his brother.

relationship: parallel judgment reaching young people, men and women
rationale: Jeremiah 28 enumerates young man, virgin, man and woman in the scattering. Jeremiah 6 likewise extends judgment across young people and the seizure of man and woman, while also naming children and elders.
source_text: In you I will scatter young man and virgin; in you I will scatter man and woman.

target_units.text: And I filled up My fury and held back and did not bring them to an end. I will pour it upon little children outside and upon a gathering of young men together, because man and woman will be seized, the elder with one full of days.

relationship: parallel repayment of Babylon for harm to Zion
