rationale: Jeremiah promises repayment to Babylon for the evils done against Zion. The psalm's remembrance of Jerusalem's destruction is followed by an address to daughter Babylon concerning repayment of what she gave the speakers.
source_text: I will repay Babylon and all the Chaldeans who live there for all the evils they did against Zion before your eyes, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Remember, Lord, Edom’s sons on Jerusalem’s day, those saying, “Empty her, empty her, down to the foundation within her!”
Daughter Babylon, miserable one, happy is the one who will repay you the repayment you gave us.

relationship: parallel downfall of Babylon portrayed as exalted and destructive
rationale: Jeremiah's mountain that ruins the earth is rolled down from the rocks. Isaiah's lament against Babylon's king likewise combines lofty ambition, descent and devastation of the inhabited world; its heavenly and underworld images differ from the burning mountain.
source_text: I am against you, ruined mountain that ruins the whole earth. I will stretch My hand against you, roll you down from the rocks, and make you like a burned mountain.

target_units.text: How the dawn-bearer who rises in the morning fell from heaven! The one dispatching to all the nations was shattered to earth.
You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.
I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’
But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.
Those who see you will marvel at you and say, ‘Is this the person who provoked the earth, shook kings,
who made the whole inhabited world deserted and pulled down the cities, who did not release those in captivity?’

relationship: contrast between Babylon's unusable stones and Zion's foundation
rationale: Jeremiah denies taking a cornerstone or foundation stone from ruined Babylon. Isaiah promises a precious cornerstone in Zion's foundations, placing the same building vocabulary in a contrasting promise for a different city.
source_text: They will certainly not take from you a cornerstone or a foundation stone, for you will be a ruin for ever, says the Lord.

target_units.text: therefore thus says the Lord: “Behold, I will place in Zion’s foundations a costly, chosen, precious cornerstone, in her foundations, and whoever trusts in it will certainly not be ashamed.

relationship: parallel locust-like multitude in a destructive advance
rationale: Jeremiah orders horses brought against Babylon like a multitude of locusts. Judges likewise pictures destructive invaders as locusts in multitude and emphasizes their uncountable numbers, while naming camels rather than horses.
source_text: Raise a signal on the earth; sound a trumpet among the nations. Consecrate nations against her; give orders against her to Ararat’s kingdoms from Me and to the Ashkenazites. Set up arrow batteries against her; bring up horses against her like a multitude of locusts.

target_units.text: For they and their livestock came up, bringing their tents; they arrived like locusts in multitude. They and their camels were beyond numbering, and they entered Israel’s land to ruin it.

relationship: parallel mustering of the Medes against Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah summons nations against Babylon and names the Medes' king among the mobilized power. Isaiah's Babylon oracle likewise explicitly says God is rousing the Medes against its addressee.
source_text: Consecrate nations against her: the king of the Medes and of all the earth, his leaders and all his generals.

target_units.text: Behold, I am rousing the Medes against you, who do not value silver or have need of gold.

relationship: parallel divine purpose to desolate Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah connects the shaken earth with the Lord's purpose to make Babylon uninhabited. Isaiah likewise announces the Lord rising against her and making Babylonia deserted, with the loss of her remnant and offspring.
source_text: The earth was shaken and suffered, for the Lord’s purpose rose against Babylon, to make Babylon’s land a ruin, no longer inhabited.

target_units.text: “I will rise against them,” says the Lord Sabaoth, “and destroy their name, remnant and offspring”—thus says the Lord—
“and make Babylonia deserted, so that hedgehogs dwell there; she will become nothing. I will make her a muddy abyss for destruction.”

relationship: parallel failed defenses, women imagery and burning barriers
rationale: Jeremiah describes crushed military power, defenders becoming like women, burned dwellings and shattered bars. Nahum likewise compares a city's people with women as its gates open to enemies and fire consumes its bars.
source_text: Babylon’s warrior has ceased fighting; they will sit there in confinement. Their power was crushed; they became like women. Her dwellings were burned; her bars were shattered.

target_units.text: Look, your people within you are like women! The gates of your land will open wide to your enemies, and fire will consume your bars.

relationship: parallel threshing imagery for judgment upon hostile power
rationale: Babylon's royal houses are to be threshed like a prepared floor as harvest approaches. Micah likewise pictures hostile nations gathered like sheaves on a threshing floor and commands Zion to thresh them, applying agricultural processing to defeated powers.
source_text: For thus says the Lord: The houses of Babylon’s king will be threshed like a threshing floor ready for use; a little longer, and her harvest will come.

target_units.text: But they did not know the Lord’s thought or understand His counsel, for He gathered them like sheaves of a threshing floor.

Rise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze. With them you will melt down nations and grind many peoples fine; you will dedicate their multitude to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.

relationship: parallel dragon imagery for an imperial ruler
rationale: Jeremiah likens Nebuchadnezzar's devouring to a dragon swallowing and filling its belly. Ezekiel explicitly calls Pharaoh a great dragon among his rivers; both depict imperial rulers through the creature, though Ezekiel emphasizes capture rather than swallowing.
source_text: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon devoured me, divided me, seized me, a thin vessel. He swallowed me like a dragon, filled his belly, and drove me from my luxury.

target_units.text: “Son of man, fix your face upon Pharaoh king of Egypt and prophesy against him and against all Egypt,
and say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against Pharaoh, the great dragon seated among his rivers, who says, ‘The rivers are mine, and I made them.’
I will put traps in your jaws and fasten the fish of your river to your fins. I will bring you up from the midst of your river, and all the fish of your river,

and I will cast you down quickly, and all the fish of your river. You will fall on the face of the plain; you will certainly not be gathered or wrapped for burial. I have given you for food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of heaven.

relationship: parallel complaint seeking repayment for Jerusalem's suffering
rationale: Zion and Jerusalem call for their miseries and blood to fall upon Babylon and the Chaldeans. The psalm likewise remembers Jerusalem's destruction and anticipates Babylon receiving the repayment she gave the speakers.
source_text: My toils and miseries be upon Babylon, the woman dwelling in Zion will say; my blood be upon the Chaldeans who live there, Jerusalem will say.

target_units.text: Remember, Lord, Edom’s sons on Jerusalem’s day, those saying, “Empty her, empty her, down to the foundation within her!”
Daughter Babylon, miserable one, happy is the one who will repay you the repayment you gave us.

relationship: parallel divine drying of waters
rationale: Jeremiah promises to lay Babylon's sea waste and dry her spring as God judges Zion's adversary. Isaiah likewise depicts God declaring the abyss desolate and drying its rivers; the named bodies of water and surrounding setting differ.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: I will judge your adversary and avenge you; I will lay her sea waste and dry her spring.

target_units.text: He says to the abyss, ‘You will be desolate, and I will dry your rivers’;

relationship: parallel enduring lack of habitation in Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah says Babylon will become a ruin without inhabitants. Isaiah likewise names Babylon and denies habitation through generations, expanding the same city's announced desolation.
source_text: Babylon will become a ruin and will not be inhabited.

target_units.text: Babylon, which is called glorious by the king of the Chaldeans, will be as when God overturned Sodom and Gomorrah.
She will not be inhabited for everlasting time, nor will people ever enter her through many generations. Arabs will certainly not pass through her, and shepherds will certainly not rest in her.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between lions and slaughtered flock animals
rationale: The group is first pictured as roused lions and lions' cubs. Two units later God brings them down like lambs, rams and young goats for slaughter, reversing the animals' threatening posture into vulnerability.
source_text: Together they were roused like lions and like lions’ cubs.

target_units.text: I will bring them down like lambs to slaughter and like rams with young goats.

relationship: related drink and sleep imagery for divine judgment
rationale: Jeremiah portrays Babylon's people receiving a stupefying drink and everlasting sleep. Isaiah likewise joins the Lord's cup of anger, drunkenness and helpless sleeping, but calls Jerusalem to rise and promises removal of her cup rather than everlasting sleep.
source_text: In their heat I will give them a drink and make them drunk, so that they are stupefied and sleep an everlasting sleep and certainly do not rise, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, rise, Jerusalem, you who drank the cup of anger from the Lord’s hand. You drank out and emptied the cup of falling, the bowl of anger.
There was no one to comfort you among all your children you bore, and no one to take your hand among all your sons you raised.
These two confront you—who will grieve with you?—fall and crushing, famine and sword. Who will comfort you?
Your sons are helpless, sleeping at every way out like a half-boiled beet, full of the Lord’s anger, exhausted because of the Lord God.
Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.
Thus says the Lord God who judges His people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling, the bowl of anger. You will not drink it again.

relationship: parallel flock animals as imagery of divine slaughter
rationale: Jeremiah pictures people brought down like lambs, rams and young goats for slaughter. Isaiah's judgment upon Idumea similarly uses lambs, male goats and rams in the Lord's sacrifice, applying animal-slaughter imagery to another threatened people.
source_text: I will bring them down like lambs to slaughter and like rams with young goats.

target_units.text: The Lord’s sword was filled with blood, thickened with lambs’ fat and the fat of male goats and rams, for the Lord has a sacrifice in Bosor and a great slaughter in Idumea.
The stout ones will fall with them, and rams and bulls; the earth will become drunk with blood and be filled with their fat.

relationship: repeated lament over Babylon's fallen worldwide prominence
rationale: Both ask how Babylon became a ruin among nations. Jeremiah 28 calls her the whole earth's boast captured, while Jeremiah 27 calls her the whole earth's hammer shattered, distinct images of the same reversal.
source_text: How the boast of the whole earth was captured and hunted! How Babylon became a ruin among the nations!

target_units.text: How the hammer of the whole earth was snapped and shattered! How Babylon became a ruin among nations!

relationship: parallel waters covering a threatened land and city
rationale: Jeremiah 28 pictures the sea covering Babylon with its waves. Jeremiah 29 likewise describes rising waters becoming a flood over land, city and inhabitants in a different oracle; the comparison concerns the covering-water image.
source_text: The sea rose over Babylon with the sound of its waves, and she was covered.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Waters are rising from the north and will become a flooding torrent. It will flood the land and its fullness, the city and those living in it. People will cry out, and all the land’s inhabitants will shout aloud.

relationship: repeated exclusion of human habitation from devastated places
rationale: Babylon's cities become waterless and untrodden, without human habitation. Jeremiah 30 similarly describes the courtyard as perpetually untrodden, with no person settling or living there, while adding ostriches to its description.
source_text: Her cities became a waterless and untrodden land; not one person will live there, nor will any human lodge there.

target_units.text: The courtyard will become an abode for ostriches, untrodden for ever. No person will settle there; no human being will live there.

relationship: parallel rescue from a devouring oppressor's mouth
rationale: God promises to bring what Babylon swallowed out of her mouth. Ezekiel likewise promises to rescue His sheep from the shepherds' mouth so they are no longer food, using the same devouring-and-release image for oppressive power.
source_text: I will exact vengeance on Babylon and bring what she swallowed out of her mouth. Nations will certainly no longer gather to her.

target_units.text: thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am against the shepherds. I will require My sheep from their hands and turn them aside from shepherding My sheep. The shepherds will no longer feed them. I will rescue My sheep from their mouth, and they will no longer be food for them.

relationship: related worldwide scope of fallen wounded people
rationale: Jeremiah 28 places wounded men from all the earth in Babylon. Jeremiah 32 describes the Lord's wounded lying from one part of the earth to another; the international scope corresponds while the distribution of the wounded differs.
source_text: And in Babylon wounded men from all the earth will fall.

target_units.text: And those wounded by the Lord on the Lord’s day will lie from one part of the earth to another. They will certainly not be buried; they will be dung upon the earth’s face.

relationship: parallel remembrance of Jerusalem while away from her
rationale: Those escaping far away must remember the Lord and hold Jerusalem in their hearts. The psalm likewise depicts people in Babylon remembering Zion and insisting that Jerusalem not be forgotten, a particular counterpart in displacement.
source_text: You who escape from the land, go on; do not stand still. You who are far away, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem rise in your hearts.

target_units.text: For David. By Babylon’s rivers, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.
Upon the willows in her midst we hung our instruments.
For there those who took us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who led us away for a hymn: “Sing us some of Zion’s songs.”
How can we sing the Lord’s song on foreign land?
If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be forgotten.
May my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem first at the beginning of my gladness.

relationship: parallel shame over foreigners entering holy places
rationale: Jeremiah's speakers report dishonor because foreigners entered the Lord's holy places. The psalm likewise says nations entered God's inheritance and defiled His holy temple, then describes the community's reproach and ridicule.
source_text: We were disgraced, for we heard our reproach; dishonor covered our face. Foreigners entered our holy places, the Lord’s house.

target_units.text: A psalm for Asaph. God, nations entered Thine inheritance; they defiled Thy holy temple; they made Jerusalem into a fruit-watchman’s hut.
They made the dead bodies of Thy servants food for the birds of heaven, the flesh of Thy holy ones for the beasts of the earth.
They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.
We became a reproach to our neighbors, sneering and ridicule to those around us.

relationship: related judgment upon Babylon's carved images
rationale: Jeremiah promises vengeance upon Babylon's carvings. Isaiah likewise describes fallen Bel and shattered Dagon, with carved images carried as burdens into captivity, giving a concrete depiction of defeated manufactured objects.
source_text: Therefore days are coming, says the Lord, when I will exact vengeance on her carvings, and wounded men will fall throughout her land.

target_units.text: Bel fell; Dagon was shattered. Their carved images became a burden for wild and domestic animals. Lift them, bound together, as a load for one who is weary
and hungry and exhausted, without strength at all; they cannot be saved from war, and they themselves were led captive.

relationship: parallel heavenly-height ambition brought down
rationale: Even Babylon's ascent to heaven and fortified height will not stop God-sent destroyers. Isaiah's lament against Babylon's king likewise describes ambition to ascend above stars and clouds, followed by descent to Hades.
source_text: Even if Babylon rises as high as heaven and fortifies the height of her strength, those who destroy her will come from Me, says the Lord.

target_units.text: You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.
I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’
But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.

relationship: repeated great shattering in the Chaldeans' land
rationale: The cry in Babylon and great shattering in Chaldea closely correspond to Jeremiah 27's sound of war and great shattering in the same land. The two descriptions locate the heard calamity explicitly in Babylon's domain.
source_text: A sound of crying in Babylon, a great shattering in the Chaldeans’ land!

target_units.text: A sound of war and great shattering in the Chaldeans’ land!

relationship: related water-like national noise brought to an end
rationale: Jeremiah likens Babylon's loud voice to many waters before its silencing. Isaiah likewise compares nations' roaring with abundant rushing water and describes displacement and a swiftly ended threat; its later pronouns are not used to identify Babylon.
source_text: For the Lord destroyed Babylon and silenced her loud voice sounding like many waters; He gave her voice over to destruction.

target_units.text: Woe, the multitude of many nations! Like a surging sea, so you will be troubled, and the back of many nations will roar like water.

Many nations are like abundant water, like much water violently rushing down. He will drive him away and pursue him far off, like chaff-dust when people winnow before wind, and like wheel-dust carried by a squall.
Toward evening there will be mourning; before morning it will be gone. This is the portion of those who plundered you, an inheritance for those who took possession of you.

relationship: parallel divine repayment upon Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah 28 explains Babylon's military misery through God's repayment of her recompense. Jeremiah 27 likewise commands repayment according to her works, doing to her what she did, a shared measure of judgment upon the named city.
source_text: For misery came upon Babylon. Her warriors were captured; their bow is terrified, because God repays them; the Lord repays her recompense.

target_units.text: Give orders against Babylon to many, to everyone drawing a bow. Encamp against her all around; let none of her people escape. Repay her according to her works; do to her all she did, for she resisted the Lord, Israel’s holy God.

relationship: same-chapter repetition of judgment through divine intoxication
rationale: Jeremiah 28:57 names leaders, wise men and generals who will be made thoroughly drunk. The earlier announcement likewise says God will give a stupefying drink, adding the image of everlasting sleep.
source_text: He will make her leaders and wise men and generals thoroughly drunk, says the King, whose name is the Lord Almighty.

target_units.text: In their heat I will give them a drink and make them drunk, so that they are stupefied and sleep an everlasting sleep and certainly do not rise, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel demolition of Babylon's wall
rationale: Jeremiah 28 announces the utter demolition of Babylon's broadened wall and burning of its high gates. Jeremiah 27 likewise describes her fallen battlements and demolished wall; this counterpart does not reinterpret the later statement that peoples will not labor in vain.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Babylon’s wall was broadened; it will be utterly demolished, and her high gates burned. Peoples will not labor in vain, and nations will perish at the beginning.

target_units.text: Clap against her! Her hands were disabled, her battlements fell, and her wall was demolished. For this is vengeance from God; take vengeance upon her. Do to her as she did.

relationship: parallel dating to Zedekiah's fourth year
rationale: The instructions associated with Seraiah's journey to Babylon are dated to Zedekiah's fourth year. Jeremiah 35 dates Hananiah's distinct public speech to that same regnal year and its fifth month, connecting chronology without conflating the events.
source_text: The word the Lord commanded Jeremiah the prophet to tell Seraiah son of Neriah son of Maaseiah when he went from Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was an official over gifts.

target_units.text: And in the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fifth month, Hananiah son of Azzur, the false prophet from Gibeon, said to me in the Lord’s house before the priests and all the people:

relationship: parallel written preservation of Jeremiah's judgment words
rationale: Jeremiah writes Babylon's announced evils in one scroll. Jeremiah 43 likewise commands a roll containing the delivered oracles and describes Baruch writing from Jeremiah's mouth, there with a broader scope including Judah and all nations.
source_text: Jeremiah wrote in one scroll all the evils that would come upon Babylon, all these words written against Babylon.

target_units.text: Take a writing roll and write on it all the words I have delivered to you as oracles concerning Jerusalem, Judah, and all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah king of Judah until today.
Perhaps Judah’s house will hear all the calamities I intend to bring upon them, so that they turn from their evil way and I may be merciful toward their injustices and sins.
Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and he wrote on a writing roll, from Jeremiah’s mouth, all the Lord’s words which He had delivered to him as oracles.

relationship: parallel delegated reading of written prophetic words
rationale: Jeremiah instructs Seraiah to read the written words when he reaches Babylon. Jeremiah 43 likewise records his instruction to Baruch to read a roll to the people, while specifying the Lord's house and a fast day rather than Babylon.
source_text: Jeremiah said to Seraiah: When you arrive in Babylon, you will see and read all these words,

target_units.text: Jeremiah instructed Baruch, I am under guard and cannot enter the Lord’s house.
Read from this roll in the people’s hearing at the Lord’s house on a fast day, and read it to all Judah’s people coming from their city.
Perhaps their appeal for mercy will fall before the Lord, and they will turn from their evil way, for great are the Lord’s wrath and anger which He has pronounced against this people.
Baruch did everything Jeremiah instructed him, reading the Lord’s words from the document in the Lord’s house.

relationship: repeated desolation of Babylon without human or animal inhabitants
rationale: The instructed prayer recalls God's word to make the place a perpetual ruin without people or livestock. Jeremiah 27 announces Babylon's ruin with the corresponding exclusion of human and animal inhabitants.
source_text: and say, Lord, Lord, Thou spakest against this place to destroy it and leave no inhabitants in it, from human to livestock, for it will be a ruin for ever.

target_units.text: A nation came up against her from the north; it will make her land a ruin, with no one living in it, from human to livestock.

relationship: parallel enacted signs of a city's irreversible destruction
rationale: The stone-bound scroll thrown into the Euphrates is explained in 28:64 as Babylon's sinking without rising. Jeremiah 19 similarly uses the breaking of a jar to portray a people and city smashed beyond healing, with a different object and city.
source_text: When you finish reading this scroll, bind a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates,

target_units.text: And smash the jar before the eyes of the men going out with you,
and say: Thus says the Lord: This is how I will smash this people and this city, as an earthenware vessel is smashed that cannot be healed again.

relationship: shared sinking imagery for the defeat of an imperial power
rationale: Babylon's announced sinking is illustrated by the scroll cast into the river in the preceding unit. Exodus celebrates Pharaoh's force covered by the sea and sinking like a stone, a corresponding defeat image rather than the same event.
source_text: and say, Thus Babylon will sink and certainly not rise because of the evils I am bringing upon her.

target_units.text: Pharaoh’s chariots and his host He has cast into the sea; chosen riders, officers, He has drowned in the Red Sea.
With the sea He covered them; they sank into the deep as a stone.

relationship: parallel overflowing waters threatening land and inhabitants
rationale: Jeremiah describes northern waters becoming a torrent over the land and city. Isaiah likewise depicts the Assyrian king's advance as strong river water and an encampment filling the country's breadth, an explicit military application of the water image.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Waters are rising from the north and will become a flooding torrent. It will flood the land and its fullness, the city and those living in it. People will cry out, and all the land’s inhabitants will shout aloud.

target_units.text: therefore, behold, the Lord brings up against you the river’s strong and abundant water—the king of the Assyrians and his glory. He will ascend every ravine of yours and walk over every wall of yours,
and he will remove from Judea a person able to lift a head or someone strong enough to accomplish anything. His encampment will fill the breadth of your country. God is with us.”

relationship: parallel sounds of horses, wheels and chariots in calamity
rationale: Jeremiah emphasizes the sound of the onrush, hooves, chariots and wheels before describing failed parental response. Nahum likewise lists shaking wheels, a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot amid slaughter; it does not repeat the fathers-and-sons detail.
source_text: At the sound of his onrush, of the hooves of his feet, the shaking of his chariots, and the noise of his wheels, fathers did not turn back to their sons, because their hands failed,

target_units.text: The sound of whips and the sound of shaking wheels, of a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot,
and of a mounting horseman, a flashing sword and glittering weapons, a multitude of slain and a grievous fall! There was no limit to her nations, and they will weaken in their bodies

relationship: parallel judgment naming Tyre and Sidon
rationale: Jeremiah names Tyre and Sidon among the coastal powers facing destruction. Joel likewise addresses both cities and announces repayment for their treatment of Judah and Jerusalem, giving a particular counterpart for the named coastal pair.
source_text: on the day coming to destroy all the people of another tribe. I will obliterate Tyre and Sidon and all the remainder of their assistance, for the Lord will destroy the survivors of the islands.

target_units.text: What have you to do with Me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of foreigners? Are you repaying Me a recompense? Or do you bear a sharp grudge against Me? I will speedily repay your recompense upon your heads,
because you took My silver and gold and brought My chosen and beautiful things into your temples,
and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so as to thrust them out of their own borders.
Look, I am rousing them from the place to which you sold them, and I will repay your recompense upon your heads,
and I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them into captivity to a nation far away, because the Lord has spoken.”

relationship: parallel judgment naming Gaza and Ashkelon
rationale: Jeremiah describes baldness upon Gaza and the casting away of Ashkelon. Zephaniah likewise announces Gaza's plundering and Ashkelon's disappearance; the target does not supply the baldness or Anakim detail.
source_text: Baldness has come upon Gaza; Ashkelon and the survivors of the Anakim have been cast away. How long will you strike,

target_units.text: For Gaza will be plundered and Ashkelon will disappear; Ashdod will be cast out at midday and Ekron uprooted.

relationship: same-chapter question and answer about the Lord's sword
rationale: The speaker asks how long the Lord's sword will remain unquiet and urges it to return to its sheath. The following unit answers that it cannot be quiet because the Lord commanded its action against Ashkelon and the coast.
source_text: sword of the Lord? How long will you not be quiet? Return to your sheath; rest and be lifted away!

target_units.text: How will it be quiet? The Lord commanded it to rise against Ashkelon, against the coastal places, against those remaining.

relationship: parallel sword action governed by divine command
rationale: Jeremiah 29 explains the sword's continuing action through the Lord's command against the coast. Jeremiah 27 likewise orders the sword to avenge and carry out everything God commands, there in Babylon's judgment.
source_text: How will it be quiet? The Lord commanded it to rise against Ashkelon, against the coastal places, against those remaining.

target_units.text: Go fiercely against her and her inhabitants. Take vengeance, sword, and make her disappear, says the Lord; do everything I command you.

relationship: parallel loss of wisdom in Idumea and Teman
rationale: Jeremiah announces the loss of wisdom and discerning counsel in Teman within the Idumea oracle. Obadiah likewise predicts the destruction of Idumea's wise people and understanding, then names Teman's terrified warriors.
source_text: For Idumea, thus says the Lord: There is no longer wisdom in Teman; counsel perished from the discerning; their wisdom went away.

target_units.text: On that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the wise from Idumea and understanding from Mount Esau.
Your warriors from Teman will be terrified, so that a person may be removed from Mount Esau,

relationship: same-chapter command to go deep to dwell
rationale: Both units instruct the addressed inhabitants to go deep to dwell. Jeremiah 30:2 addresses Dedan amid visitation, while 30:25 addresses those in the courtyard before Babylon's planned attack; the repeated instruction connects distinct local warnings.
source_text: Their place was deceived. Go deep to dwell, inhabitants of Dedan, for he did difficult things; I brought them upon him at the time I visited him.

target_units.text: Flee far away; go deep to dwell, you who stay in the courtyard, for Babylon’s king planned counsel against you and devised a purpose against you.

relationship: parallel grape-gatherer and night-thief comparisons with differing wording
rationale: Both Idumea oracles compare loss with grape gathering and thieves at night. Jeremiah says the gatherers leave no remnants, whereas Obadiah asks whether gatherers would not leave a gleaning; the shared comparisons should not erase that verbal distinction.
source_text: For grape gatherers came to you; they will leave you no remnants. Like thieves by night they will lay their hand upon you.

target_units.text: If thieves came in to you, or robbers by night, where would you have been cast away? Would they not have stolen enough for themselves? And if grape gatherers came in to you, would they not have left a gleaning?

relationship: parallel exposure of Esau's secrets and hostility from close associates
rationale: Jeremiah describes Esau dragged out, secrets uncovered and destruction through brother and neighbor. Obadiah likewise speaks of Esau searched out and hidden things seized, followed by betrayal from covenant partners and men at peace with him.
source_text: For I dragged Esau away and uncovered their secrets; they certainly cannot hide. They perished by the hand of his brother and his neighbor, and it is not possible

target_units.text: How Esau has been searched out, and his hidden things seized!
All the men of your covenant sent you out as far as your borders; the men at peace with you opposed you and prevailed over you. They set ambushes beneath you. There is no understanding in them.

relationship: parallel insistence that judgment's cup cannot be refused
rationale: Jeremiah 30 addresses one as acquitted yet denies acquittal and insists upon drinking. Jeremiah 32 likewise says unwilling recipients certainly will drink and argues that judgment beginning with God's named city does not leave others exempt.
source_text: For thus said the Lord: Those for whom there was no law to drink the cup drank it. And you, though acquitted, certainly will not be acquitted, for you will certainly drink.

target_units.text: And when they are unwilling to receive the cup from your hand to drink, say: Thus said the Lord: You will certainly drink.
Because I am beginning to bring harm in the city upon which My name was named, and you will certainly not be cleansed, because I am summoning a sword against those dwelling upon the earth.

relationship: parallel divine oath by Himself announcing judgment
rationale: The Lord swears by Himself before announcing lasting desolation in the Idumea oracle. Amos likewise introduces a city's removal through the Lord's oath by Himself, there condemning Jacob's arrogance.
source_text: For I swore by Myself, says the Lord, that you will become an untrodden place, a reproach, and a curse in her midst, and all her cities will be deserted for ever.

target_units.text: For the Lord swore by Himself: “I abhor all Jacob’s arrogance and have hated his regions; I will remove the city with all who inhabit it.”

relationship: parallel report from the Lord and summons of nations to war
rationale: Both Idumea passages report hearing from the Lord and a dispatch or messengers sent among nations. Both then summon an uprising for battle against the addressed land, a close correspondence in the oracle's announced mobilization.
source_text: I heard a report from the Lord, and He sent messengers to the nations: Gather and come against her; rise for war!

target_units.text: The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord God to Idumea: I heard a report from the Lord, and He sent a dispatch to the nations: “Rise up! Let us rise against her for battle!”

relationship: parallel lowering of Idumea among nations
rationale: Both passages say God has made the addressed people small or insignificant among nations and despised or dishonored. Their common Idumea setting makes this a particular counterpart to the loss of national standing.
source_text: I made you small among nations, easily despised among people.

target_units.text: Look, I have made you insignificant among the nations; you are greatly dishonored.

relationship: parallel pride, eagle-nest imagery and divine abasement
rationale: Jeremiah joins the heart's insolence, rocks, a high hill and an eagle-like nest before God's promise to bring the addressee down from there. Obadiah similarly joins heart-pride, rock dwellings and an eagle's nest among stars, also followed by God bringing the addressee down.
source_text: Your playfulness assailed you; your heart’s insolence destroyed holes in rocks and seized the strength of a high hill. For he raised his nest like an eagle; from there I will bring you down.

target_units.text: The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who camp in holes in the rocks, raising his dwelling high and saying in his heart, “Who will bring me down to the ground?”
If you soar like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel enduring desolation in Idumea's judgment
rationale: Jeremiah announces Idumea made untrodden, with passersby hissing. Isaiah's Idumea oracle likewise predicts a land deserted for generations, there described through sulfur, pitch and continuing fire rather than the passersby's response.
source_text: Idumea will become an untrodden place; everyone passing by her will hiss.

target_units.text: Her ravines will turn to pitch, her earth to sulfur, and her land will burn like pitch
night and day. It will not be quenched for an everlasting time, and her smoke will rise upward. For generations and a long time she will be deserted.

relationship: explicit comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah's overthrow
rationale: Jeremiah directly compares Idumea's desolation with the overthrow of Sodom, Gomorrah and neighboring places. Genesis narrates the Lord overthrowing those cities and the surrounding country, supplying the stated comparison's event.
source_text: As Sodom, Gomorrah, and her neighboring places were overturned, said the Lord Almighty, no person will settle there, and no human being will live there.

target_units.text: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of the heaven;
and He overthrew those cities, and all the surrounding country, and all that lived in the cities, and all that sprang from the earth.

relationship: repeated lion and Jordan imagery with questions about resisting God
rationale: Both describe a lion coming from the Jordan into Aitham's place and ask who can resist God or what shepherd can stand before Him. The closely corresponding language appears in the distinct Idumea and Babylon oracles.
source_text: Like a lion he will come up from Jordan’s midst into Aitham’s place, for I will quickly drive them away from her. Appoint the young men over her. For who is like Me? Who will resist Me, and what shepherd can stand before Me?

target_units.text: Like a lion he will come up from the Jordan into Aitham’s place, for I will quickly drive them away from her and appoint every young man over her. For who is like Me? Who will resist Me, and what shepherd can stand before Me?

relationship: parallel divine counsel expressed through threatened sheep and dwelling
rationale: The Lord's counsel against Idumea and Teman is followed by small sheep and their dwelling made untrodden. Jeremiah 27 likewise joins counsel against Babylon with lambs and disappearing pasture, retaining different places and exact consequences.
source_text: Therefore hear the Lord’s counsel that He planned against Idumea and His purpose against Teman’s inhabitants: Surely the smallest sheep will be swept together; surely their dwelling will be made untrodden over her.

target_units.text: Therefore hear the Lord’s counsel that He has planned against Babylon and His purposes against the resident Chaldeans: Surely the lambs of their sheep will be destroyed; surely pasture will disappear from them.

relationship: parallel earth shaking and a far-reaching cry at a fall
rationale: The Idumea oracle describes earth shaking at the fall and a cry heard at the sea. The Babylon oracle similarly joins the earth's shaking at capture with a cry heard among nations.
source_text: For at the sound of their fall the earth shook, and your cry was heard at the sea.

target_units.text: For at the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth will shake, and a cry will be heard among the nations.

relationship: parallel eagle-like assault upon fortifications
rationale: Jeremiah depicts an eagle stretching wings over Idumea's fortifications. Deuteronomy likewise compares an approaching nation with an eagle and announces the collapse of trusted fortified walls, while addressing Israel rather than Idumea.
source_text: Like an eagle he will look and stretch his wings over her fortifications. That day Idumea’s strong men’s hearts will be like the heart of a woman in labor.

target_units.text: The Lord shall bring against you a nation from afar, from the end of the earth, as the swooping of an eagle, a nation whose speech you shall not understand,
a nation shameless of countenance, which shall not regard the face of the aged, nor have mercy upon the young.

And it shall consume the offspring of your cattle and the produce of your land, leaving you neither grain, nor wine, nor oil, nor the herds of your cattle, nor the flocks of your sheep, until it destroys you.

And it shall wear you down in all your cities, until your high and fortified walls wherein you trust are cast down throughout all your land; and it shall afflict you in all your cities which the Lord your God has given you.

relationship: territorial background to Gad's challenged inheritance
rationale: Jeremiah asks why Melchom took Gad and whether their people will live in their cities. Joshua explicitly records an inheritance for Gad, including territory near Ammon and Rabbah, supplying background to the oracle's challenge about the rightful heirs.
source_text: For Ammon’s sons, thus said the Lord: Are there no sons in Israel, or have they no one to inherit? Why did Melchom take Gad, and will their people live in their cities?

target_units.text: Moses gave an inheritance to the sons of Gad according to their divisions.
Their borders were Jazer, all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the sons of Ammon, as far as Aroer facing Rabbah,
and from Heshbon to Ramoth toward Mizpah, and Betonim and Mahanaim, as far as the borders of Debir;

and in Emek: Beth-haram, Bethanabra, Succoth, and Zaphon, and the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon. The Jordan shall form the boundary as far as a part of the Sea of Chinnereth beyond the Jordan on the east.
This was the inheritance of the sons of Gad according to their divisions—their cities and their settlements.

relationship: parallel war and fire against Ammon's Rabbah
rationale: Jeremiah announces war against Rabbath and fire upon her altars in the Ammon oracle. Amos likewise announces fire upon Rabbah's walls amid war-shouting and the captivity of her leadership; the burned structures are described differently.
source_text: Therefore days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make the din of wars heard against Rabbath. They will become an untrodden place and a destruction, her altars will be burned with fire, and Israel will receive his rule.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they ripped open the pregnant women of the Gileadites in order to enlarge their borders.
I will kindle fire upon Rabbah’s walls, and it will devour her foundations with shouting on the day of war; she will be shaken on the day of her end.
Her kings will go into captivity, their priests and their rulers together,” says the Lord.

relationship: parallel deportation with priests and rulers in Ammon's judgment
rationale: Jeremiah says Melchom will go into deportation with priests and rulers. Amos's Ammon oracle likewise sends kings, priests and rulers into captivity together, preserving its different named subjects rather than equating Melchom with the kings.
source_text: Shout aloud, Heshbon, for Gai perished! Cry out, daughters of Rabbath; put on sackcloth, be seized with distress, and beat yourselves over Melchom, for he will go into deportation, his priests and rulers together.

target_units.text: Her kings will go into captivity, their priests and their rulers together,” says the Lord.

relationship: contrast to confidence that treasures provide security
rationale: The Ammon oracle questions the dishonored daughter's confidence in treasure and her challenge about who could come against her. Zephaniah explicitly denies that silver and gold can rescue people in the Lord's wrath, countering that kind of confidence.
source_text: Why do you exult in the plains of the Anakim, daughter of dishonor, trusting in her treasures and saying, Who will come against me?

target_units.text: Their silver and gold will certainly not rescue them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of His jealousy all the earth will be consumed, for He will bring completion and haste upon all the earth’s inhabitants.

relationship: parallel dispersal without anyone gathering
rationale: Jeremiah announces surrounding fear and people scattered with no gatherer. Isaiah likewise depicts fugitives and a wandering sheep without anyone gathering, with each turning toward his own people and land.
source_text: I am bringing fear upon you, said the Lord, from all your surroundings. You will be scattered, each straight ahead, and there will be no one gathering.

target_units.text: Those left will be like a fleeing little gazelle and a wandering sheep, with no one to gather them, so that each turns back to his own people and hastens to his own country.

relationship: parallel prophetic judgment specifically naming Kedar
rationale: Jeremiah introduces the attack upon Kedar associated with Babylon's king. Isaiah likewise announces the failure of Kedar's glory and few remaining arrows of its strong sons, giving another particular judgment upon the named people without identifying the campaigns.
source_text: For Kedar, queen of the courtyard, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck. Thus said the Lord: Rise and go up against Kedar, and fill the sons of Kedem!

target_units.text: For thus the Lord said to me: “Yet one year, like a hired worker’s year, and the glory of Kedar’s sons will fail,
and the remaining arrows of Kedar’s strong sons will be few, because the Lord, Israel’s God, has spoken.”

relationship: parallel taking of tents, sheep and camels in war
rationale: Jeremiah predicts the taking of tents, sheep, equipment and camels from the addressed people. Chronicles similarly records tents handed over and camels and sheep captured from the Hagaraeans and their allies, in a different battle.
source_text: They will take their tents and sheep, their garments, all their equipment, and camels for themselves. Call destruction against them on every side!

target_units.text: and they prevailed over them, and the Hagaraeans and all their tents were given into their hands. For they cried to God in the battle, and He listened to them because they hoped in Him.
They captured their baggage: five thousand camels, two hundred fifty thousand sheep, two thousand donkeys, and one hundred thousand human lives.

relationship: same-chapter repeated command to go deep to dwell
rationale: Before Babylon's planned attack, the courtyard's inhabitants must flee far and go deep to dwell. The earlier Dedan warning uses the same unusual dwelling instruction amid visitation, without making the two locations identical.
source_text: Flee far away; go deep to dwell, you who stay in the courtyard, for Babylon’s king planned counsel against you and devised a purpose against you.

target_units.text: Their place was deceived. Go deep to dwell, inhabitants of Dedan, for he did difficult things; I brought them upon him at the time I visited him.

relationship: parallel attack upon a settled people without defensive barriers
rationale: Jeremiah describes a stable nation living in refreshment with no doors, pins or bars. Ezekiel likewise records a plan to attack peaceful inhabitants of a land without walls, bars or doors, with plunder as the purpose.
source_text: Rise and go up against a stable nation living in refreshment, with neither doors nor pins nor bars; they lodge alone.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: On that day words will rise in your heart, and you will devise evil plans,
and say, “I will go up against an abandoned land; I will come upon those resting quietly and dwelling in peace, all living in a land with no wall or bars, and they have no doors,”

to take plunder and strip their spoils, to turn your hand against the desolate land that was inhabited and against a nation gathered from many nations, acquiring possessions, dwelling upon the earth’s navel.

relationship: parallel scattering to every wind
rationale: Jeremiah 30 threatens to winnow the addressed people to every wind alongside the plundering of their animals. Jeremiah 25 similarly scatters Elam among winds from heaven's four ends, giving a particular dispersion image applied to another people.
source_text: Their camels will become plunder and their numerous livestock destruction. I will winnow them to every wind, those shorn before their faces; from every side of them I will bring their rout, said the Lord.

target_units.text: I will bring upon Elam four winds from heaven’s four ends and scatter them among all these winds. There will be no nation where Elam’s outcasts do not come.

relationship: repeated exclusion of human habitation from devastated places
rationale: The courtyard becomes perpetually untrodden, without people settling or living there. Jeremiah 28 similarly describes Babylon's cities as waterless and untrodden with no human dwelling; the ostrich detail belongs to Jeremiah 30.
source_text: The courtyard will become an abode for ostriches, untrodden for ever. No person will settle there; no human being will live there.

target_units.text: Her cities became a waterless and untrodden land; not one person will live there, nor will any human lodge there.

relationship: parallel collapse announced for Damascus
rationale: Jeremiah depicts Damascus growing feeble and fleeing in terror. Isaiah likewise explicitly announces Damascus's removal as a city and the loss of its kingdom, a particular counterpart to the city's failing strength.
source_text: Damascus grew feeble and turned to flight; trembling seized her.

target_units.text: The utterance against Damascus. Behold, Damascus will be removed from the cities and become a ruin,
abandoned for everlasting time, a bed and resting place for flocks, with no one pursuing.

There will no longer be a stronghold for Ephraim to flee to, nor a kingdom in Damascus, and the Syrians’ remainder will perish; for you are no better than Israel’s sons and their glory. Thus says the Lord Sabaoth.

relationship: repeated fall of young men in squares and warriors
rationale: The Damascus oracle announces young men falling in its squares and all its warriors falling. Jeremiah 27 uses the same paired announcement against Babylon, while the cities remain distinct.
source_text: Therefore young men will fall in your squares, and all your warriors will fall, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Therefore her young men will fall in her squares, and all her warriors will be thrown down, said the Lord.

relationship: parallel fire against Damascus and the son of Ader
rationale: Jeremiah announces fire in Damascus's wall consuming the quarters of Ader's son. Amos likewise sends fire against Hazael's house to consume the foundations of the son of Ader and shatters Damascus's bars.
source_text: I will kindle fire in Damascus’s wall, and it will devour the quarters of Ader’s son.

target_units.text: I will send fire into Hazael’s house, and it will devour the foundations of the son of Ader,

and I will shatter Damascus’s bars and destroy inhabitants from the Plain of On. I will cut down a tribe from the men of Harran, and the people of Syria, called by name, will be taken captive,” says the Lord.

relationship: parallel Moab oracle naming Nebo or Nabau in calamity
rationale: Jeremiah opens Moab's oracle with Nebo's ruin among other cities. Isaiah likewise opens with Moab's ruin and then calls for wailing over Nabau; the correspondence concerns the Moab oracle and that closely corresponding place-name, not every city Jeremiah lists.
source_text: For Moab, thus said the Lord: Woe to Nebo, for she perished! Kiriathaim was taken; Amath was disgraced and defeated.

target_units.text: The utterance against Moab’s country. In a night Moab’s country will perish, for in a night the wall of Moab’s country will perish.
Grieve over yourselves, for Debon too will perish. Where your altar is, there you will go up to weep. Over Nabau of Moab’s country, wail: baldness upon every head, every arm cut.

relationship: parallel national wound that cannot be healed
rationale: Jeremiah 31 says there is no healing for Moab, before announcing evil against her. Jeremiah 28 likewise says Babylon was treated but not healed, applying the unhealed-nation image to another land.
source_text: There is no longer healing for Moab, a boast in Heshbon. They devised evils against her: We cut her off from a nation, and she will certainly cease. A sword will walk behind you.

target_units.text: We treated Babylon, but she was not healed. Let us leave her; let each of us go to our own land, for her judgment reached heaven and rose to the stars.

relationship: parallel Moabite cry of destruction associated with Horonaim or Aroniim
rationale: Jeremiah locates a cry of destruction and great shattering at Horonaim. Isaiah's Moab lament similarly locates a cry of destruction and shaking on Aroniim's road; the native place-name forms are preserved in each passage.
source_text: For a sound of people crying out comes from Horonaim: destruction and great shattering!

target_units.text: Moab’s heart cries within her as far as Segor, for she is a three-year-old heifer. On Louith’s ascent they will go up toward you weeping; along Aroniim’s road destruction and shaking cry out.

relationship: parallel Moabite cry associated with Zogora or Segor
rationale: Jeremiah announces Moab's shattering and commands an announcement in Zogora. Isaiah likewise joins Moab's cry with Segor, within its detailed account of the land's distress; neither wording needs to be replaced with another version's account of children crying.
source_text: Moab was shattered; announce it in Zogora.

target_units.text: Moab’s heart cries within her as far as Segor, for she is a three-year-old heifer. On Louith’s ascent they will go up toward you weeping; along Aroniim’s road destruction and shaking cry out.

relationship: parallel weeping and cry of shattering on a Moabite road
rationale: Jeremiah says Alaoth was filled with weeping, then describes going up weeping on Horonaim's road and a heard cry of shattering. Isaiah likewise joins a weeping ascent, named Louith, with a cry of destruction along Aroniim's road; it does not make Alaoth an explicitly named ascent in Jeremiah.
source_text: For Alaoth was filled with weeping; he will go up weeping on Horonaim’s road. You heard a cry of shattering:

target_units.text: Moab’s heart cries within her as far as Segor, for she is a three-year-old heifer. On Louith’s ascent they will go up toward you weeping; along Aroniim’s road destruction and shaking cry out.

relationship: shared wild-donkey image associated with wilderness dwelling
rationale: Jeremiah urges fugitives to save their lives and says they will be like a wild donkey in the wilderness. Job explicitly describes the free wild donkey whose dwelling God made in the wilderness, supplying the animal-and-habitat comparison without making Job's animal a fugitive nation.
source_text: Flee and save your lives, and you will be like a wild donkey in the wilderness!

target_units.text: Who is the one who let the wild donkey go free, and who loosened its bonds?
I made its dwelling the wilderness, and its encampments the salt marsh,
laughing at the city’s crowded bustle, and not hearing a tax collector’s reproach;
it will examine mountains for its pasture and seek after every green thing.

relationship: parallel deportation with priests and rulers
rationale: Jeremiah 31 sends Chemosh into deportation with priests and rulers. Jeremiah 30 similarly sends Melchom with priests and rulers, a close formulation applied to the distinct Moab and Ammon oracles.
source_text: Because you trusted in your fortifications, you too will be seized. Chemosh will go into deportation, his priests and rulers together.

target_units.text: Shout aloud, Heshbon, for Gai perished! Cry out, daughters of Rabbath; put on sackcloth, be seized with distress, and beat yourselves over Melchom, for he will go into deportation, his priests and rulers together.

relationship: same-chapter comprehensive judgment upon Moab's cities
rationale: Jeremiah 31:8 says destruction comes to every city and no city escapes. The concluding city-list unit extends judgment to all Moab's cities far and near, making explicit the same comprehensive geographic scope.
source_text: Destruction will come upon every city; no city will be saved. The valley will perish and the plain be destroyed, as the Lord said.

target_units.text: upon Kerioth, Bosor, and all Moab’s cities, far and near.

relationship: parallel curse for failure to participate in the Lord's warfare
rationale: Jeremiah curses one who does the Lord's works negligently and withholds his sword from blood. Deborah and Barak's song likewise curses Meroz because its inhabitants did not come to the Lord's help, then calls the Lord their helper, mighty among warriors; both concern their particular warfare settings.
source_text: Accursed is one who does the Lord’s works carelessly, removing his sword from blood.

target_units.text: ‘Curse Meroz,’ said the Lord’s messenger, ‘utterly curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to the Lord’s help. The Lord is our helper, mighty among warriors.’

relationship: same-chapter contrast between undisturbed vessels and coming tilters
rationale: Moab rested from childhood and did not pour from vessel to vessel; his taste remained and scent did not fade. The next unit answers that condition by promising tilters who will tilt him and thin his vessels; its final clause concerns horns rather than shattered jars.
source_text: Moab rested from childhood and trusted in his glory. He did not pour from vessel to vessel or go into deportation. Therefore his taste remained in him and his scent did not fade.

target_units.text: Therefore days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send him tilters who will tip him, thin out his vessels, and cut up his horns.

relationship: same-chapter vessel judgment answering Moab's prior ease
rationale: The promised tilters and treatment of vessels answer the preceding description of Moab resting and not pouring from vessel to vessel. The connection is the text's explicit vessel imagery, not an imported account of jars being smashed.
source_text: Therefore days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send him tilters who will tip him, thin out his vessels, and cut up his horns.

target_units.text: Moab rested from childhood and trusted in his glory. He did not pour from vessel to vessel or go into deportation. Therefore his taste remained in him and his scent did not fade.

relationship: historical background to Israel's confidence in Bethel
rationale: Jeremiah compares Moab's shame concerning Chemosh with Israel's shame over Bethel, their hope. Kings records Jeroboam's two golden heifers, one placed in Bethel, and calls the resulting practice sin, supplying the named sanctuary's background.
source_text: Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, as Israel’s house was ashamed of Bethel, their hope, having trusted in them.

target_units.text: The king took counsel, went, and made two golden heifers. He said to the people, “Let your going up to Jerusalem be enough. Behold, your gods, Israel, who brought you up from Egypt!”
He placed one in Bethel and put the other in Dan.
This matter became a sin. The people went before the one as far as Dan.

relationship: related warning against boasting in strength
rationale: Jeremiah 31 challenges the claim to be strong and mighty in warfare. Jeremiah 9 explicitly forbids the strong person to boast in strength and directs boasting toward understanding the Lord, addressing the same claimed basis of confidence.
source_text: How will you say, We are strong, and a man strong for warfare?

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Let no wise man boast in his wisdom, let no strong man boast in his strength, and let no rich man boast in his wealth,
but let whoever boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am the Lord, doing mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth, because in these is My will, says the Lord.

relationship: parallel destruction of a nation's young men
rationale: Jeremiah 31 announces Moab's destruction and its chosen young men going to slaughter. Jeremiah 27 likewise announces Babylon's young men falling in its squares and all its warriors being thrown down; the nations remain distinct.
source_text: Moab perished, his city, and his choice young men went down to slaughter.

target_units.text: Therefore her young men will fall in her squares, and all her warriors will be thrown down, said the Lord.

relationship: parallel insistence that the day of calamity is near and swift
rationale: Jeremiah says Moab's day is near and its evil very swift. Zephaniah likewise describes the Lord's great day as near and coming very swiftly, a close temporal warning without identifying every event in the two oracles.
source_text: Moab’s day is near to coming, and his calamity is very swift.

target_units.text: For the Lord’s great day is near, near and very swift. The sound of the Lord’s day is bitter and harsh; it is appointed mighty.

relationship: parallel shattered staff or destroyed rod in a national lament
rationale: Jeremiah calls observers to lament Moab's shattered renowned staff, the rod of grandeur. Ezekiel's lament about Israel's ruler likewise describes a rod of strength and its destruction, ending with no such rod left; its vine-and-fire account differs from Moab's wording.
source_text: Move in lament for him, all who surround him, all who know his name. Say, How the renowned staff is shattered, the rod of grandeur!

target_units.text: She had a rod of strength for a tribe of leaders; it rose in her size among the trunks, and it saw her size among the multitude of her branches.
She was broken off in wrath and thrown to the ground. The scorching wind dried her choice parts; her rod of strength was punished and dried up. Fire consumed her.
Now they have planted her in the wilderness, in a waterless land,
and fire went out from a rod of her choice parts and devoured her, and there was no rod of strength in her. A tribe is for a parable of lament, and it will become a lament.”

relationship: parallel command for a city's honored figure to descend and sit
rationale: Jeremiah commands resident Dibon to come down from glory and sit in dampness. Isaiah similarly commands Babylon's virgin daughter to come down and sit on the ground, contrasting former honor with abasement while preserving dampness versus ground.
source_text: Come down from glory and sit in dampness, resident Dibon. Be crushed, for Moab perished; he came up against you, ruining your fortification.

target_units.text: “Come down and sit on the ground, virgin daughter Babylon. Enter darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, for you will no longer be called tender and pampered.

relationship: parallel roadside questioning of a fugitive about a disaster
rationale: Jeremiah tells Aroer's inhabitants to stand on the road and ask the fugitive what happened. Samuel narrates Eli sitting by the road and asking the escaped battle messenger what happened, providing a concrete scene of receiving disaster news rather than the same event.
source_text: Stand on the road and look, you who live in Aroer. Ask the one fleeing and the one being saved, and say, What happened?

target_units.text: A Benjaminite man ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that day, with his garments torn and earth on his head.
He came, and behold, Eli was sitting on the seat by the gate, watching the road, for his heart was distraught over God’s ark. The man entered the city to report, and the city cried out.
Eli heard the sound of the cry and said, “What is this crying sound?” The man hurried in and reported to Eli.
Eli was ninety years old. His eyes were fixed, and he could not see. Eli said to the men standing around him, “What is the sound of this uproar?”
The man hurried up to Eli and said to him, “I am the one who has come from the camp. I fled from the battle line today.” He said, “What happened, child?”
The young man answered and said, “The men of Israel have fled before the foreigners. There has been a great slaughter among the people. Both your sons are dead, and God’s ark has been captured.”

relationship: parallel Moabite ruin answered by public lament
rationale: Jeremiah announces Moab's shame and shattering and commands lament and an announcement of its ruin. Isaiah likewise describes Moab's overnight ruin and people mourning in public places, with named cities raising their voices.
source_text: Moab was ashamed, for he was shattered. Wail and cry out; announce at Arnon that Moab perished.

target_units.text: The utterance against Moab’s country. In a night Moab’s country will perish, for in a night the wall of Moab’s country will perish.
Grieve over yourselves, for Debon too will perish. Where your altar is, there you will go up to weep. Over Nabau of Moab’s country, wail: baldness upon every head, every arm cut.
In her squares put on sackcloth and beat yourselves in mourning; upon her roofs and in her lanes all of you wail with weeping.
For Hesebon and Eleale have cried out; their voice was heard as far as Iassa. Therefore Moab’s loins cry out; her soul will know.

relationship: territorial background to the Misor, Jahzah and Mophath list
rationale: Jeremiah places judgment upon the Misor and names Jahzah and Mophath among its places. Joshua's account of Reuben's inheritance likewise names the Misor, Jahaz and Mephaath, supplying earlier territorial context while retaining the different native spellings.
source_text: Judgment is coming into the land of Misor: upon Chailon, Jahzah, and Mophath,

target_units.text: Their borders were from Aroer facing the Arnon ravine, and the city in the Arnon ravine, and all the Misor,
as far as Heshbon and all the cities in the Misor, Dibon, Bamoth-baal, and the house of Beelmon,
Jahaz, Kedemoth, and Mephaath,

relationship: parallel Moab oracle naming Dibon and Nebo with corresponding forms
rationale: Jeremiah names Dibon and Nebo among places under judgment. Isaiah's Moab oracle likewise names Debon and Nabau in its announcement of ruin and wailing; the connection is the particular city pair, with each native spelling preserved.
source_text: upon Dibon, Nebo, and the house of Deblathaim,

target_units.text: Grieve over yourselves, for Debon too will perish. Where your altar is, there you will go up to weep. Over Nabau of Moab’s country, wail: baldness upon every head, every arm cut.

relationship: earlier settlement background for Kiriathaim
rationale: Jeremiah includes Kiriathaim among the places facing judgment. Numbers records Reuben's sons building Kiriathaim with Heshbon and Elealeh, giving earlier settlement background for this one city rather than for every place in Jeremiah's unit.
source_text: upon Kiriathaim, the house of Gamol, and the house of Maon,

target_units.text: And the sons of Reuben built Heshbon, Elealeh, and Kiriathaim,

relationship: same-chapter judgment extending to every Moabite city
rationale: The city list concludes by including all cities of Moab far and near. Jeremiah 31:8 had already said destruction would reach every city and none would escape, supplying the earlier comprehensive claim developed by this list.
source_text: upon Kerioth, Bosor, and all Moab’s cities, far and near.

target_units.text: Destruction will come upon every city; no city will be saved. The valley will perish and the plain be destroyed, as the Lord said.

relationship: parallel breaking of horns as loss of wicked strength
rationale: Jeremiah announces Moab's horn broken and effort shattered. The psalm likewise promises to break sinners' horns while raising the righteous person's horns, a particular shared image of strength brought down without repeating the statement about effort.
source_text: Moab’s horn was broken and his effort shattered.

target_units.text: And I will break together all sinners’ horns; and the righteous person’s horns will be raised.

relationship: parallel Moab included among nations made to drink judgment
rationale: Jeremiah 31 commands that Moab be made drunk because it magnified itself against the Lord. Jeremiah 32 names Moab among the nations receiving the cup and commands its recipients to drink and become drunk; Jeremiah 31's hand-striking clause is not replaced with the target's vomiting.
source_text: Make him drunk, for he magnified himself against the Lord. Moab will strike with his hand and become a laughingstock himself.

target_units.text: and Idumea, the Moabite land, and Ammon’s sons;
and all Tyre’s kings, Sidon’s kings, and the kings across the sea;
and Dedan, Teman, Ros, and everyone shorn about his face;
and all the mixed populations lodging in the wilderness;
and all Elam’s kings and all the Persian kings;
and all the kings from the east, far and near, each with his brother, and all the kingdoms upon the face of the earth.
And say to them: Thus said the Lord Almighty: Drink, get drunk, and vomit; you will fall and certainly not rise before the sword I am sending among you.

relationship: parallel charge that Moab reproached God's people
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether Israel was an object of laughter to Moab and exposes its response against him. Zephaniah explicitly condemns Moab's reproaches against God's people and its arrogant self-exaltation, supplying the same particular national offense.
source_text: Was not Israel a laughingstock to you? Was he found in your thefts, that you made war on him?

target_units.text: I heard Moab’s reproaches and the Ammonites’ blows, with which they reproached My people and exalted themselves against My borders.

Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of powers, the God of Israel, Moab will be like Sodom and the Ammonites like Gomorrah, and Damascus abandoned like a heap on a threshing floor and vanished forever. My people’s remnant will plunder them; My nation’s remnant will inherit them.
This will be theirs for their arrogance, because they reproached and exalted themselves against the Lord Almighty.

relationship: shared image of a dove sheltered at a rock
rationale: Jeremiah reports that Moab's inhabitants left the cities, lived among rocks and became like doves nesting among rocks at a pit's mouth. The Song likewise addresses a dove in the rock's shelter; its affectionate invitation differs from this report of displaced inhabitants.
source_text: Moab’s inhabitants left the cities and lived among rocks. They became like doves nesting among rocks at a pit’s mouth.

target_units.text: and come, my dove, in the shelter of the rock, close to the outer wall. Show me your face and let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet and your face lovely.

relationship: parallel report of Moab's arrogance and insolence
rationale: Both passages introduce what has been heard of Moab's insolence and then describe its arrogance. Jeremiah adds the heart being lifted up, while Isaiah adds a statement about divination.
source_text: I heard Moab’s insolence; he acted very insolently—his insolence and arrogance—and his heart was lifted up.

target_units.text: We heard Moab’s insolence—exceedingly insolent. You raised up your arrogance. Your divination is not so,

relationship: parallel lament extending throughout Moab
rationale: Jeremiah commands lament for Moab on every side and calls for mourning at Kiradas of drought. Isaiah likewise says Moab will wail and all will wail in Moab; its further reference to Deseth is preserved rather than equated with Jeremiah's locality.
source_text: Therefore wail over Moab from every side; cry out over the men of Kiradas of drought.

target_units.text: not so. Moab will wail, for all in Moab’s country will wail. You will ponder for Deseth’s residents and not be ashamed.

relationship: parallel weeping for the Sibmah or Sebama vine like Jazer or Iazer
rationale: The Jeremiah passage compares weeping for Sibmah's vine with Jazer's weeping and describes destruction falling upon summer fruit and grape gatherers. The Isaiah passage similarly describes weeping like Iazer for Sebama's vine and harvest and vintage trampled down, retaining the differing objects and name forms.
source_text: Like the weeping for Jazer, I will weep for you, vine of Sibmah. Your branches crossed the sea and reached Jazer. Destruction fell upon your summer fruit and your grape gatherers.

target_units.text: Therefore I will weep like Iazer’s weeping for Sebama’s vine. He felled your trees, Hesebon and Eleale, because I will trample upon your grain harvest and vintage, and all will fall.

relationship: parallel loss of Moab's vineyard gladness and winepress celebration
rationale: Jeremiah describes joy boiled away from Moab, wine upon the presses and the absence of treading and the aidad shout. Isaiah likewise removes gladness from vineyards and says people will not tread wine in the vats; it does not supply Jeremiah's morning-and-evening wording.
source_text: Joy and gladness were boiled away from Moab’s land, and wine was upon your winepresses. They did not tread in the morning or in the evening; they did not make an aidad shout.

target_units.text: Gladness and exultation will be removed from your vineyards; in your vineyards they will certainly not rejoice or tread wine into the vats, for it has ceased.

relationship: parallel named Moabite cries and ruined waters
rationale: Jeremiah joins Heshbon and Elealeh's cry with other Moabite places and says Nebrim's water will be burning. Isaiah likewise joins Hesebon and Eleale's voices with the country's distress and Nemrim's water, there described as deserted rather than burning.
source_text: From Heshbon’s cry as far as Elealeh, their cities raised their voice; from Zogor to Horonaim and Aglath-salisia, for even Nebrim’s water will become a burning.

target_units.text: For Hesebon and Eleale have cried out; their voice was heard as far as Iassa. Therefore Moab’s loins cry out; her soul will know.
Moab’s heart cries within her as far as Segor, for she is a three-year-old heifer. On Louith’s ascent they will go up toward you weeping; along Aroniim’s road destruction and shaking cry out.
Nemrim’s water will be deserted, and her grass cease; for there will be no green grass.

relationship: related failure of Moabite worship in calamity
rationale: Jeremiah announces that the Lord will destroy Moab as he ascends to an altar and burns incense to his gods. Isaiah likewise describes Moab's labor at altars and prayer to handmade objects as unable to rescue, connecting the named nation's worship with its failure in judgment.
source_text: I will destroy Moab, says the Lord, as he goes up to an altar and burns incense to his gods.

target_units.text: It will turn to your shame, because Moab labored at the altars and will enter her handmade objects to pray; it will certainly not be able to rescue him.

relationship: parallel bodily lament for Moab compared with an instrument
rationale: The Jeremiah passage compares the heart's sound for Moab with flutes. The Isaiah passage likewise compares the belly for Moab with a lyre; the bodily location and instrument differ, but both turn internal grief for the same nation into a musical simile.
source_text: Therefore my heart, Moab, will hum like flutes; my heart will hum like a flute for Kiradas’s people. Therefore what he acquired perished from a person.

target_units.text: Therefore my belly will sound like a lyre for Moab, and my inward parts like a wall that you renewed.

relationship: parallel baldness and sackcloth in Moabite mourning
rationale: Both Moab oracles mention bald heads and sackcloth. Jeremiah also describes shaved beards and hands beating themselves, whereas Isaiah speaks of cut arms; the shared mourning scene does not make those additional actions identical.
source_text: They will shave every head in every place; every beard will be shaved, all hands will beat themselves, and on every waist is sackcloth.

target_units.text: Grieve over yourselves, for Debon too will perish. Where your altar is, there you will go up to weep. Over Nabau of Moab’s country, wail: baldness upon every head, every arm cut.
In her squares put on sackcloth and beat yourselves in mourning; upon her roofs and in her lanes all of you wail with weeping.

relationship: parallel nation or city pictured through a broken vessel
rationale: The Lord compares His shattering of Moab with a vessel that has no use. The enacted sign in Jeremiah 19 breaks a jar and explains the Lord's breaking of the people and city through that earthenware vessel, there emphasizing that it cannot be healed again.
source_text: And on all Moab’s rooftops and in her squares—for I shattered Moab, says the Lord, like a vessel for which there is no use.

target_units.text: And smash the jar before the eyes of the men going out with you,
and say: Thus says the Lord: This is how I will smash this people and this city, as an earthenware vessel is smashed that cannot be healed again.

relationship: parallel defeated people becoming neighbors' object of derision
rationale: Jeremiah describes Moab turning its back in shame and becoming an object of laughter and anger to surrounding people. The psalm likewise laments becoming neighbors' reproach and mockery to those around, speaking there for God's people rather than Moab.
source_text: How he has changed! How Moab turned his back! He was ashamed, and Moab became a laughingstock and an object of resentment to all around her.

target_units.text: We became a reproach to our neighbors, sneering and ridicule to those around us.

relationship: same-chapter seized fortresses answering misplaced confidence
rationale: Jeremiah 31:7 identifies confidence in fortifications before announcing seizure. Jeremiah 31:41 says Akkarioth was taken and fortifications seized, developing that announced collapse of security without requiring a separate historical identification.
source_text: Akkarioth was taken and the fortifications seized.

target_units.text: Because you trusted in your fortifications, you too will be seized. Chemosh will go into deportation, his priests and rulers together.

relationship: same-chapter repeated charge of self-exaltation against the Lord
rationale: Both units explain Moab's humiliation through the explicit charge that he magnified himself against the Lord. Jeremiah 31:26 orders drunkenness, while 31:42 says Moab will perish from being a multitude, preserving the differing consequences.
source_text: Moab will perish from being a multitude, for he magnified himself against the Lord.
